The Buddha told Ānanda:
"In the worlds of the ten directions, among all devas and humans, should there be those who with a sincere heart vow to be born in that land..."
There are three classes of people. As for those of the highest class: they leave their homes and renounce desire to become śramaṇas;

they resolve their minds on bodhicitta and single-mindedly and exclusively recollect Amitāyus Buddha; they cultivate various meritorious virtues and vow to be born in that land. Such sentient beings as these—
At the time of their death, Amitāyus Buddha, together with a great assembly, will appear before them.
They shall then be reborn in that land by following that Buddha, spontaneously manifesting through transformation within lotuses made of the seven treasures.

There they will abide in the stage of non-retrogression, possessing courageous wisdom and sovereign supernatural powers. Therefore, Ānanda, those who wish to see Amitāyus Buddha in this present life should—
They give rise to the mind of unsurpassed bodhi and cultivate meritorious deeds, vowing to be born in that land. As for those of middle capacity:
among the devas and humans of the worlds of the ten directions, there are those who with a sincere heart vow to be born in that land;

although they cannot become śramaṇas or extensively cultivate great merit, they should give rise to the mind of unsurpassed bodhi and single-mindedly and exclusively keep in mind the Immeasurable [Life].
O Amitāyus Buddha! To whatever extent one cultivates goodness, observes the precepts and fasts, erects stupas and images,

provides food for śramaṇas, hangs silk banners, lights lamps, scatters flowers, and burns incense— dedicating these merits with the vow to be born in that land— that person, at the time of death, will see the Buddha Amitāyus manifest his transformed body,
complete with radiant light and the marks and signs of a true Buddha, appearing before them together with a great assembly.
In the presence of others, they shall immediately follow the Transformation Buddhas to be reborn in that land, dwelling in the stage of non-retrogression;
their merit and wisdom will be next only to those of the upper grade. As for those of the lower grade:

among the devas and people of the worlds of the ten directions, should there be those who with a sincere heart wish to be reborn in that land, even if they are unable to perform various meritorious deeds, they should resolve to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta.
If one directs one’s mind single-mindedly, even for as little as ten recitations of the name of Amitāyus Buddha, vowing to be born in his land;

or if, upon hearing the profound Dharma, one rejoices with faith and delight, giving rise to no doubt or hesitation; or even if one recollects that Buddha for but a single thought-moment—one shall likewise attain rebirth there.
Their merit and wisdom will be next only to those of the middle grade.
The *Amitābha Sūtra*: "Śāriputra,
if there be good sons or good daughters who, upon hearing the teaching of Amitābha Buddha, hold fast to his name—
whether for one day, two days, three days, four days, five days, six days, or..."
For seven days, with a single mind free from distraction, when that person approaches the end of life, Amitābha Buddha, together with the assembly of holy beings, will appear before them.
At the time of death, this person’s mind will not be inverted, and they will immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha Buddha.
Śāriputra, because I see these benefits, I speak these words. If there are sentient beings who hear...
Those who speak thus should make a vow to be born in that land.
In the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, the Buddha told Ānanda and Vaidehī: "The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, are the Dharma-realm body; they enter into all assemblies."
It arises within the mind’s conceptualization. Therefore, when you all bring the Buddha to mind through conceptualization, this very mind is the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics;
this mind creates the Buddha, and this mind is the Buddha. The ocean of the Tathāgatas’ perfect and universal knowledge arises from the mind’s conceptualization.
For this reason, you should single-mindedly fix your mindfulness and clearly contemplate that Buddha, the Tathāgata.
The Arhat, Samyak-saṃbuddha. One who wishes to visualize that Buddha should first form a mental image;
with eyes both closed and open, one sees a precious image with the color of Jāmbūnada gold, seated upon that flower.

Once the image is seen sitting there, the mind’s eye opens, and one perceives clearly and distinctly the adornments of the seven treasures in the Land of Ultimate Bliss—the jeweled ground, the jeweled ponds, and the jeweled trees.

Rows [of deities], with celestial jeweled canopies covering them from above, and nets of various jewels filling the void of space—seeing these things, one should perceive them with extreme clarity, as if looking at the palm of one's hand.
Having seen these things, one should further imagine a great lotus flower to the left of the Buddha, and another great lotus flower to the right of the Buddha. One should visualize Avalokiteśvara.
Visualize an image of the Bodhisattva Guṇarāja seated upon a flower-seat to the left; he is also golden in color, no different from before.
Visualize an image of the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta seated upon a flower-seat to the right. When this visualization is accomplished, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas all emit light;
that light is golden in color and illuminates the various jewel-trees. Beneath each and every tree, there are likewise three lotus flowers, and upon each of these lotus flowers—
In each [lotus] there is one Buddha and two Bodhisattva images, filling that land entirely.

When this visualization is accomplished, the practitioner shall hear the sounds of flowing water and light, as well as the various jewel-trees, ducks, wild geese, and mandarin ducks all preaching the sublime Dharma. This occurs both upon emerging from and entering into meditative concentration.
Constantly hearing the sublime Dharma,
the Śūraṅgama Sūtra’s Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, together with fifty-two bodhisattvas of his same rank, immediately rose from their seats and [bowed] with their heads...

He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and addressed the Buddha, saying: "I recall that in the past, during kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Immeasurable Light (*Amitābha*).
Twelve Tathāgatas followed one after another for the duration of that kalpa; the last of these Buddhas was named Surpassing the Light of Sun and Moon (*Sūryacandraprabhāsa-vyatikrama*)."

That Buddha taught me the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha. It is like this: suppose there is one person who is single-mindedly intent on remembering, and another person who is single-mindedly intent on forgetting.
These two people may meet and yet not meet, or see each other and yet not see. Because these two people remember one another, their mutual mindfulness is profound.
In this way, from birth to birth, they are like a form and its shadow, never diverging or differing. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions cherish sentient beings as a mother remembers her child.
If the child has fled and wandered away, though the mother remembers him, what can she do? But if the child remembers his mother...
Just as when a mother remembers her child, the mother and child do not remain separated throughout their successive lives;

so too, if sentient beings with sincere hearts remember the Buddha and recite his name, they will certainly see the Buddha in the present and the future. They will be near the Buddha, and without relying on expedient means, their minds will open of themselves.
Just as the body of one who has been anointed with incense bears its fragrance, this is called the Adornment of Fragrant Light.

When I was originally on the ground of practice, I entered the patience of non-arising through the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha; now, within this world-system, I gather those who mindfully recite the Buddha's name and lead them back to the Pure Land.
The Buddha asked Yuantong: "I have no choice; I simply withdraw all six sense faculties, maintaining a continuous stream of pure mindfulness to attain samādhi.
This is the foremost method.
— *Mahāvaipulya Bhadrapāla-paripṛcchā Sūtra* (Dafangdeng Jixianhu Jing)
Bhadrapāla, those sons of good family or daughters of good family sit upright with focused mindfulness, concentrating their thoughts on that Tathāgata,
Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Amitābha— his such physical marks and signs, his such majestic deportment, his such assembly, and his such preaching of the Dharma—
continuing with single-minded persistence in succession without confusion, whether for a day or even for a night. Thus...
Whether it be for seven days and seven nights, that person will certainly behold the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Amitābha.
If they cannot see him during the day, then during the night or within a dream, Amitābha Buddha will surely manifest.
Furthermore, Bhadrapāla, it is like when men or women in this world travel far away.
In another country, while in a dream, he sees his original home. At that time, he truly does not know whether it is day or night, nor does he know whether it is inside or outside.
At that moment, all the faculties of this person’s eyes cannot be obstructed by walls, fences, stones, or mountains;
even the most profound darkness and gloom do not hinder them. O Bhadrapāla, such is the case for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
The mind being without obstruction is likewise so. When one is in right mindfulness,
all the Sumeru Kings, the Cakravāḍa and Mahācakravāḍa mountains,
and even all other Black Mountains (Kṛṣṇaparvata) within those various Buddha-fields cannot act as obstructions for this faculty of sight, nor can they obscure this mind.
However, this person has not actually attained the divine eye by which they can see that Buddha, nor do they possess the divine ear by which they can hear the sound of his Dharma.
Furthermore, it is not that they travel there by means of supernatural powers to reach that Dharma-realm, nor do they pass away from this world to be reborn before that Buddha.

Rather, while remaining truly within this very world, they have accumulated mindfulness and cultivated their practice over a long period; because their contemplation has become clear and sharp, in the end—
They shall behold that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Amitābha, surrounded by the Saṅgha;
within that assembly of Bodhisattvas, they may see themselves listening to the Dharma there, and having heard it, they shall remember, uphold, and practice it.
At times, they shall further obtain the opportunity to reverently prostrate, honor, and make offerings to that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Amitābha.
Only after this does that person arise from this samādhi. Having emerged from contemplation, they reflect in succession upon what was seen and heard, and explain it extensively for others.
In the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra Spoken by Mañjuśrī*, Mañjuśrī said:
"World-Honored One, what is called the 'Samādhi of the Single Practice'? The Buddha said: "The Dharma-realm has a single characteristic."
To bind one’s attention to the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is called the Samādhi of One Practice.

If good sons or good daughters wish to enter this Samādhi of One Practice, they should first hear the Prajñāpāramitā and practice according to its teachings; only then can they enter the Samādhi of One Practice.
Just as with the conditions of the dharma-realm—non-retrogressive, indestructible, inconceivable, unimpeded, and signless—so it is for the good sons...

Son, or good daughter, if you wish to enter the Samādhi of the Single Practice, you should dwell in a secluded place, abandon all distracted thoughts, and refrain from grasping at external appearances.
Bind your mind to a single Buddha, single-mindedly reciting His name. Facing the direction where that Buddha resides, keep your body upright and directed toward Him.

If you can maintain this mindfulness of one Buddha in continuous succession from moment to moment, then within that very mindfulness, you will be able to see all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
Why is this? The merit of recollecting the virtues of a single Buddha is immeasurable and boundless; it is non-dual with the merit of immeasurable Buddhas.

The inconceivable Buddha-dharmas are equal and without distinction; all are realized as supreme perfect enlightenment through the One Suchness, fully endowed with immeasurable merit and immeasurable eloquence.
In the "Chapter on Verses of Praise in Tuṣita" of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra,
it is said that by taking the Buddha as one's object and maintaining uninterrupted, focused mindfulness, this person shall behold the Buddhas, their number equaling the extent of their own mind.
In the "Chapter on the Worthy Leader," it is said: If one constantly cultivates the pāramitās, one will be able to fulfill the Mahāyāna.

If one can fulfill the Mahāyāna, one will be able to make offerings to the Buddha according to the Dharma. If one can make offerings to the Buddha according to the Dharma, one will be able to bring to mind the Buddha with the mind.
Immovable. If one can recollect the Buddha with an unmoving mind, then one will constantly behold immeasurable Buddhas.
If one constantly beholds immeasurable Buddhas, then one sees that the body of the Tathāgata is eternally abiding.

In the *Zuochan Sanmei Jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Sitting Meditation), it is said that when a bodhisattva practices sitting meditation, they do not bring anything to mind, but contemplate only a single Buddha; thus, they immediately attain samādhi.
This is also found in the *Mulian Suowen Jing* (Sūtra of the Questions of Maudgalyāyana).
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana: "It is like the vast currents of ten thousand rivers, upon which float grasses and wood;

those in front do not look back, and those behind do not look forward, until they all converge in the great ocean. The world is also like this: although there may be the wealthy, the noble, and those who possess power, pleasure, and autonomy, none can escape birth, old age, sickness, and death.
This is solely because they do not believe in the Buddhist scriptures; when they become humans in future lives, their suffering will be even more severe."
They are unable to be born in the lands of the thousand Buddhas. For this reason, I speak of the Land of Immeasurable Life as being easy to approach and easy to attain;
yet people fail to practice for rebirth there, instead serving the ninety-six kinds of heterodox paths. I say of such people:
They are called those without eyes; they are called those without ears.

In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Nāgārjuna Bodhisattva states that the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* can eliminate various afflictions as well as the karmic offenses of previous lives. Other samādhis may [also] be able to...

There are those who can eliminate lust but cannot eliminate anger; there are those who can eliminate anger but cannot eliminate lust; there are those who can eliminate delusion but cannot eliminate both lust and anger;
and there are those who can eliminate the three poisons but cannot eliminate the karmic offenses of previous lives.

This *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*, however, can eliminate all manner of afflictions and all manner of offenses. Furthermore, the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* possesses great merit and is able to deliver [beings].

Sentient beings: when these bodhisattvas seek to deliver sentient beings, no other samādhi possesses such merit as this mindfulness of the Buddha (buddhānusmṛti) samādhi for swiftly extinguishing all transgressions.
Furthermore, the Buddha is the King of Dharma and the bodhisattvas are the generals of the Dharma;

he who is most honored and revered is solely the World-Honored Buddha. Therefore, one should constantly practice mindfulness of the Buddha. It is, for example, like a high minister who receives special imperial favor.
A favorite servant always keeps their master in mind. In the same way, a bodhisattva knows that all various merits and immeasurable wisdom are obtained from the Buddha;
because they recognize the gravity of this kindness, they constantly bring the Buddha to mind.
"Always wishing not to be separated from the Buddhas" means that in every lifetime where a bodhisattva is born, they always encounter the Buddhas. Question:

Since a bodhisattva should transform sentient beings, why do they always wish to encounter the Buddhas? Answer: This is because there are those who have not yet entered the bodhisattva stage (*bodhisattvabhūmi*) and have not yet attained *avaivartika* (non-retrogression) or received the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
If such persons distance themselves from the Buddhas, they will destroy their various roots of goodness and sink [into ruin].
Remaining within afflictions, one cannot save oneself; how then could one save others? It is like a person on a boat who, while in midstream, suffers a wreck;

wishing to ferry others across, they instead sink themselves into the water. Or it is like a small amount of hot water poured into a great pool of ice: though it melts a small portion, it instead turns back into ice.

So too, if a Bodhisattva has not yet entered the stage of the Dharma-position (*dharmatā-avasthā*) and remains far removed from the Buddhas, their meager merit, lacking skillful means, will likewise fail.
If one attempts to transform sentient beings through mere forceful effort, even if there is some slight benefit, one may instead fall back into ruin.

Although śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas possess the benefit of nirvāṇa, because they lack omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), they cannot instruct bodhisattvas. Because the Buddhas possess the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), they are able to instruct bodhisattvas.
It is like an elephant sinking in mud; no other elephant can pull it out. If a bodhisattva should enter [such a state]...
Within the midst of non-ways, only a Buddha can save one, for [the Buddha] is identical with the Great Way. Furthermore, the Bodhisattva reflects: "I have not yet attained the Buddha-eye;
I am no different from one who is blind. If I am not guided by a Buddha, I shall have no direction and will mistakenly enter other paths.
Even if I hear the Buddha-dharma, if I practice elsewhere, I will not know the proper timing for conversion nor the extent of the practices to be performed."
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva sees the Buddha—whether seeing him with the eyes or through the purity of mind—if they hear what he teaches, their mind will delight in the Dharma.

They will attain great wisdom, practice in accordance with the Dharma, and thereby achieve liberation. Since encountering the Buddha brings such immeasurable benefits as these, how could one not seek to see the Buddha with single-minded devotion?
It is like an infant who should not be separated from its mother, or like one traveling on a path who does not leave it.
Food and sustenance; in great heat, one is not separated from cool breezes and cold water; in great cold, one is not separated from fire; in crossing deep waters, one is not separated from a boat;
a sick person is not separated from a skilled physician; and a bodhisattva is not separated from the Buddhas. These matters surpass all others;
neither parents, kinsmen, friends, nor kings and celestial lords can provide such benefit as the Buddha does. The Buddha benefits all bodhisattvas.
They leave behind all places of suffering and abide in the ground of the World-Honored One. Question: How does one attain non-separation from all Buddhas? Answer:

Sentient beings possess the karmic causes and conditions of offenses from immeasurable kalpas; thus, although they practice merit, their wisdom is meager, and although they practice wisdom, their merit is meager.

When a Bodhisattva seeks the Buddha-way, they must practice the patience toward sentient beings (*sattvakṣānti*) and the patience toward phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*). Because they practice the patience toward sentient beings, [all... *Note: The source text appears to be fragmentary. The translation reflects the extant portion provided.*
By giving rise to compassion for sentient beings, one extinguishes the sins of immeasurable kalpas and attains immeasurable merit.

Because one practices the patience of dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*), one destroys the ignorance regarding all phenomena and attains immeasurable wisdom. Through the union of these two practices, one is never separated from the Buddhas in every lifetime.

Furthermore, because the Bodhisattva constantly delights in mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*), they always encounter the Buddhas whenever they cast off one body and receive another. Just as...
Sentient beings whose habitual desire is heavy receive the bodies of lustful birds; those with an excess of anger are born among venomous insects.

The Bodhisattva does not prize the worldly blessings and pleasures of a Cakravartin king among humans or devas, but contemplates only the Buddhas; therefore, he receives a physical form according to what his mind values most.
Furthermore, because the Bodhisattva constantly and skillfully cultivates the causal conditions for the Buddha-remembrance Samādhi (Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi), wherever he is born, it is always...
One encounters the Buddhas, as described in the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra*: when a bodhisattva enters this samādhi, they immediately see those born in the Land of Amitābha.
— *Mahāyāna Śraddhotpāda Śāstra*, by Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa.
Furthermore, when sentient beings first study this Dharma and seek to attain correct faith, their minds become timid and weak.

Because they dwell in this Sahā world, they fear that they will not always be able to encounter the Buddhas to personally receive them and make offerings; thus, they dread that their faith may falter.
It is difficult to achieve. For those whose minds wish to retreat, you should know that the Tathāgata possesses supreme skillful means to protect and sustain their faith;

namely, by means of the causal condition of single-minded mindfulness of the Buddha, they shall, according to their vows, be born in the buddha-fields of other directions and constantly behold the Buddha.
One will be forever separated from the evil realms. As it is said in the Sūtra:

"If a person single-mindedly contemplates Amitābha Buddha of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, and dedicates the roots of goodness they have cultivated with the vow to be born in that world, they shall immediately attain rebirth there.

Because they constantly behold the Buddha, they shall never again fall back. If one contemplates that Buddha’s Dharmakāya of True Suchness and practices this diligently and constantly, until the end..."
One will ultimately attain rebirth because one abides in right concentration.
From the *Ten Doubts Treatise*, the Great Master Zhiyi asks:
"If one resolutely seeks rebirth in the Western Land, I do not yet know what practices and deeds should be performed, nor what should serve as the seed for attaining such rebirth."
"In that land, moreover, laypeople all have wives and children and do not sever their lustful desires; can they be born there? Answer:
"Those who wish to be definitely born in the Western Land must possess two types of practice to certainly attain birth there: first, the practice of weary detachment (*vidveṣa-vidūṣaṇā*);

second, the practice of joyful aspiration (*abhinandana-prārthanā*). As for the practice of weary detachment: since beginningless time, ordinary beings have been bound by the five desires and transmigrate through the five realms."
Subjected to manifold sufferings, they do not give rise to the mind of revulsion toward the five desires, and thus have no prospect of escape.
For this reason, one should constantly contemplate this body as pus, blood, excrement, urine, and all manner of foul impurities—impure, stinking, and loathsome. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"In this city of the body, the rākṣasa of ignorance dwells; what wise person would take pleasure in such a body? Furthermore, another sūtra says:
This body is a collection of manifold sufferings; everything about it is impure. It is a yoke, a bond, an abscess, and a wound—fundamentally devoid of benefit.

This is true even up to the bodies of the gods. Whether walking or sitting, whether sleeping or awake, the practitioner should constantly contemplate this body as being nothing but suffering and devoid of pleasure, thereby engendering a deep sense of weary detachment (*nirveda*).
Even if one cannot suddenly sever attachment to a wife and the chamber of intimacy, one should gradually [do so].
He gives rise to revulsion and practices the seven contemplations on impurity: 1. This body of sexual desire arises from the affliction of craving; this is the impurity of the seed. 2.
At the time of the parents' union, the red and white elements combine; this is the impurity of conception. 3.
Within the womb, it resides below the stomach and above the large intestine; this is the impurity of the dwelling place. 4. While in the womb, it consumes only the mother’s [nutrients].
1. Blood: This is the impurity of being consumed by food. At the completion of five or ten months, [the fetus] turns its head toward the birth canal;

pus and blood emerge together in a state of foul, chaotic filth—this is the impurity of initial birth. 2. A thin skin covers the exterior, while within, pus and blood pervade every part—this is the impurity of the entire body.
3. Even after death, it becomes bloated and putrid, with bones and flesh scattered in all directions... foxes [devour it].
Wolves devour it; this is ultimate impurity. Since one's own body is thus, so too are the bodies of others.

One should develop a profound sense of weary detachment toward beloved objects, such as the bodies of men and women, and constantly contemplate their impurity. For one who can contemplate in this way, the afflictions of lust will gradually diminish.
Furthermore, one should make this vow: "May I forever leave behind the foul, putrid, and pus-filled food of the three realms."
One who is addicted to impurity—the bodies of men and women and the five desires—vows to attain the Dharma-nature birth-body of the Pure Land;
this constitutes the practice of wearying detachment (*vidveṣa*). The practice of joyful aspiration (*abhirati*) is further twofold: first, clarifying the intent for seeking rebirth;

second, contemplating the adornments and other features of that Pure Land to aspire with a joyful heart. Regarding the clarification of the intent for rebirth: the reason for seeking birth in the Pure Land is...
The Earth [Bodhisattva], desiring to rescue and deliver all sentient beings from suffering, reflected within himself: "I currently lack the power.
If I remain in this evil age where the conditions of affliction are powerful, I shall be bound by my own karma and sink into the three miserable realms, remaining there for kalpas on end.
Thus I have revolved in saṃsāra since beginningless time without ever finding rest; when, then, shall I be able to save these suffering beings? For this reason, I seek birth [in the Pure Land]."

The Pure Land. To draw near to the Buddhas and, upon realizing the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), to be able to rescue suffering sentient beings in the evil age—one must therefore attain rebirth there.

**Postscript to the Treatise on the Ten Doubts Regarding the Pure Land** by Chen Guàn The human mind is not constant, and phenomena are not fixed.

thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* speaks of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*). To doubt this is to doubt universally; thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* speaks of the ten doubts (*daśa-vicikitsā*).
Leaving doubt and entering faith, one enters once and enters forever, never departing from this state to attain the ultimate place.
The Pure Land is that ultimate place. Therein dwells the Lord of the Dharma, named Amitāyus. This Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma has never been interrupted;
yet, if doubt obstructs the ears, one is deaf and hears not; if doubt obstructs the mind, one is muddled and does not awaken.
