In accordance with the mind and responding to its measure, they manifest according to karma. Beneath the faculties of tongue and mind, within every thought-moment, there are the four characters of Amitābha Buddha.
Their sounds are distinct and can be articulated; the sound does not transcend the orifice, yet the nature of hearing is internally integrated.

The mind responds to the mechanism of the tongue, and that mechanism draws forth the root of thought. The mental orifice resides in the tongue; with every strike upon the orifice, hearing occurs, and with every mechanism, thought returns. It is lodged within the orifice.
It resides in the ear. Entering the stream from hearing, one reverses hearing to reach the refined essence; hearing becomes still and its nature is emptiness.

When these three are fused, every thought-moment is perfectly penetrating. After a long time, this eventually becomes the contemplation of consciousness-only. For those of sharp faculties, not a single thought arises.
Mind after mind has no locus; the six sense faculties are profoundly still; all consciousnesses dissolve and fall away; every phenomenon is entirely true; every gate is free from dependence.
In a mere flash, one thus achieves the True Contemplation of Reality (*yathābhūta-parīkṣā*).

For beginners and those newly learning, except for the time of exchanging greetings with guests, the time of attending to the great and small necessities of nature, and a brief pause in the midst of these, even when managing household affairs or performing various labors, one should not [let the mind wander].
Whether engaged in activity or in repose, they do not obstruct one another. With every thought and every utterance, they recite the sacred name;
how could any further perverse thoughts or evil intentions dare to sprout in the mind? Naturally, it becomes pure and free from admixture.

If one can fully restrain the six sense faculties and maintain a continuous flow of pure mindfulness, within no more than ten days or a month, one will attain samādhi—what is called "becoming a Buddha by means of one's own mind. One’s own...

The mind is the Buddha; it is this mind that perceives the Buddha. Those of superior faculties and great capacity transcend directly in a single thought-moment. For those of ordinary disposition, one must skillfully observe the expedient means.
This verse for exhorting others to make vows was composed by Master Cizhao.
All phenomena arise from the mind; all phenomena cease within the mind. Thus has our Buddha, the Great Śramaṇa, constantly proclaimed.

If one upholds the precepts but lacks faith and aspiration, they shall not be born in the Pure Land; they will only obtain the blessings of gods and humans, and when those blessings are exhausted, they will undergo the cycle of saṃsāra.

One wanders in confusion, difficult to escape; though reading the sutras, one lacks the eye of wisdom. Failing to recognize the Buddha’s profound intent, one may attain cleverness in future lives, yet with a distracted mind, it is hard to achieve liberation.
It is better to practice mindfulness of the Buddha; in this life there will be no fame or profit, and whether walking or sitting, one need not engage in many discursive thoughts.
This is Amitābha. Through the power of making vows and upholding the precepts, one dedicates [merit] toward rebirth in the Land of Bliss.

If one practices and maintains this in such a manner, not even one in a thousand will fail. Thus spoke Śākyamuni with his golden mouth; Amitābha personally embraces them, and all Buddhas protect and mind them.
The devas will protect and sustain them well; seeing these people who practice mindfulness of the Buddha, they are not far from the Buddha.

They shall sit at the site of enlightenment and turn the great wheel of Dharma, universally delivering boundless multitudes. It is like a woman of a poor household who is pregnant with a universal monarch.

The devas constantly protect her, though the poor woman herself does not know that there is a noble child within her womb. In the same way, it is with this person who practices mindfulness of the Buddha:
by recollecting the Buddha and constantly being mindful of him, they shall before long attain Buddhahood, for all Buddhas will skillfully guard and uphold them.
That person does not know for themselves, "I shall be born in the Pure Land," yet they instead desire to come back to future lives to be born once more among humans.
It is like a poor person’s house where there is a hidden treasure buried in the ground; the guardian spirit of the treasure constantly protects it, ensuring that nothing is lost.
The poor man himself does not know that within his own home there is a treasure trove; day after day he seeks work as a laborer, seeking food and clothing to sustain himself.
The mind of this person who recites the Buddha's name is just like this: they do not know that the person reciting the Buddha's name is fully endowed with the Tathāgatagarbha.
Though he himself declares that he has no portion [of merit], he instead seeks rebirth among humans. It is like a sick person’s house that possesses a truly wondrous medicine;
yet, not knowing the nature of that wondrous medicine, he cannot cure his own illness. Day after day by his bedside, he undergoes immeasurable suffering.

Now, for this person who practices mindfulness of the Buddha, the nature of the mind is likewise: though they do not know the mind that practices mindfulness of the Buddha, it can extinguish greed, anger, and delusion;
it can act as a great king of physicians; it can act as a great treasury of jewels; it can benefit and deliver all people; and it can act as a great Dharma King.
"Protecting all sentient beings, yet acting as if one were an ordinary person, one cannot be born in the Pure Land. First, observe the precepts and fasts for oneself;
in future lives, vow to be human again. By practicing the Way through successive rebirths, one may finally be born in that land. I have seen many who practice the Way."

They constantly speak in this manner: they do not praise the vows of Amitābha, nor do they accord with the Pure Land sutras. Their minds are shrouded by the obstruction of false views, making it ultimately difficult for them to attain liberation.
This is not the obstruction caused by others; it is entirely the obstruction of their own minds. Thus, they will not be born [in the Pure Land] in this present life.
One slip leads to a hundred slips. I exhort you, O practitioners: believe the words of the Tathāgata. The Buddha never speaks that which is not true;
how could these be empty or deceptive words? You should simply exert yourselves with diligence and seek the Pure Land with a single mind. It is like wind fanning a fire.
The effort required is not great; fortunately, you possess the mind of *nien-fo*. Dedicate this aspiration to transcend the triple world.

To encounter a treasure and fail to take it, or to meet with food and suffer long hunger—alas for such a great man! You do not perceive the true meaning. I now offer this brief exhortation and praise.
Pass it on from person to person; for my sake, circulate it widely. Act as the messenger of the Tathāgata; you are truly the children of all Buddhas.
This is truly called repaying the Buddha’s kindness. May all practice according to these teachings, and together be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
The Lotus School Treasure Mirror (Lianzong baojian) states that Master Yudantan, the Patriarch Cizhao, said:
"Regarding the Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection Free from Characteristics, those of superior faculties and wisdom awaken to this profound principle."

One should constantly exercise a mind of equality as vast as space, free from the marks of self, person, sentient being, or life-span. As the Sūtra says: "To be detached from all marks is itself called the Buddhas.
The Treatise states: "Self" is reckoned in terms of the internal; "person" is reckoned in terms of the external; "sentient being" takes the continuity of the preceding [moment] as its function;
and "life-span" takes the continuity of the succeeding [moment] as its meaning. Since there is no longer any clinging mind regarding internal or external, or prior or subsequent, then [all is] one.
All marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are entirely empty and quiescent. Therefore, a sutra says: "Knowing there is no self (*ātman*) or person (*pudgala*), who undergoes saṃsāra?
Furthermore, there is neither body nor mind that undergoes birth and death. This is called the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha by Detaching from Marks.

In this, one sees that the original nature of all sentient beings is identical to that of Amitābha. Thus, one neither clings to the two extremes of having marks nor being markless, nor does one fall into nihilism.
Regarding the teaching on the perception of permanence: this is the manifestation of Amitābha in every thought-moment and the appearance of Sukhāvatī everywhere before one.
To contemplate in this way is the contemplation of non-contemplation; contemplation is thus True Suchness (*tathatā*). Birth that is without birth is the Real Mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Therefore, know that non-contemplation is the departure from discursive thoughts, and the Real Mark is formlessness (*animitta*). Formlessness is non-abiding; non-abiding is entry into Buddhahood.
This realm is the unsurpassed, true, and great path of Bodhi. Upon reaching this ground, there is neither cultivation nor realization;
there is no birth-and-death to be liberated from, and no Nirvana to be sought. Both nature and characteristics are empty; the holy and the ordinary are equal.
There is no Buddha-path to be accomplished, no sentient beings to be saved, and no individual spirit to be attained. In a single thought-moment of non-action, one sits throughout the ten directions.

Severance. There is not a single dharma that is originally existent, nor a single dharma that is newly formed. Self and other mutually encompass one another; phenomena and principle are without obstruction.
Every atom is fully endowed; every world-realm is completely manifested. Such is the fundamental nature of dharmas, beyond the reach of thought or deliberation.
It may be called "the gate to nirvana on the single path of the Bhagavans of the ten directions."
The Preface to the *Chanzhi Jing* by the Distant Patriarch states: "Without Chan, there is no means to exhaust its stillness; without Chan, there is no means to deepen its illumination.
Chan and wisdom are what is meant by 'illumination of stillness'; they assist one another. Illumination does not depart from stillness, and stillness does not depart from illumination.
When there is resonance, they travel together; when there is response, they share the same destination. Cizhao says: "Still while constantly illuminating; illuminating while constantly [still]..."

Quiescence. It is eternally quiescent and eternally illuminating; this is called the Light of Eternal Quiescence. Those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha and wish to engage in Chan to see their true nature should rely solely on this method.
They must sit upright with the body straight in a clean room, clearing away distracting entanglements and severing the dust of emotional attachments.

With eyes wide open, they should neither cling to external objects nor dwell in internal concentration. When they turn the light back to illuminate themselves, both the internal and external become simultaneously quiescent. Thereafter—
Silently and continuously raise the thought "Namo Amitābha Buddha" three or five times. Turn the light back upon yourself and look within, saying:
"To see one's nature is to become a Buddha. Ultimately, which of these is my original nature, Amitābha?
Then, again, observe and examine: from where does this present single thought arise? Penetrate through this thought, and then further penetrate through this very act of observation.
"Who is it that is thus? Investigate for a long while. Again, bring to mind "Namo Amitābha Buddha. Again, look in this way; investigate in this way.
Apply yourself to the practice with urgency, never allowing for interruption. Remain alert and unclouded, like a hen brooding over her eggs.
Whether engaged in any of the four modes of deportment, likewise bring it to mind, likewise look, and likewise investigate. Suddenly, while walking, standing, sitting, or...
While lying in bed, upon hearing a sound or seeing a form, one suddenly attains clear awakening and personally beholds the Buddha Amitābha as one's own original nature.

Body and mind, internal and external, are simultaneously liberated; the entire universe and the great earth are this very Western Land. The myriad phenomena and the ten thousand forms are none other than oneself.
In stillness, there is no lack of illumination; in movement, one does not lose tranquility. Only then does one give rise to kindness and exercise compassion to guide those who have not yet awakened.

With compassion and wisdom perfectly integrated, one enters the stage of effortless practice (*anābhoga-caryā*) and attains birth in the superior grade, which is called the Land of Adornments of True Retribution (*sambhoga-kṣetra*).
One then attains the Knowledge of All Modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying, "By practicing what dharma does a bodhisattva swiftly realize [enlightenment]?"
Regarding unexcelled bodhi, the Buddha said that a bodhisattva who can correctly practice the Samādhi of the Adornment of a Single Mark will swiftly realize bodhi.
One who cultivates this practice should distance themselves from clamor and distraction, refrain from contemplating manifold marks, and single-mindedly fix their mindfulness upon a single Tathāgata.
Carefully taking up His name and skillfully contemplating His countenance and deportment, they thereby universally observe all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
One immediately attains the all-encompassing wisdom of all Buddhas. The *Ten Doubts Treatise* (Shi yi lun) of Tiantai states: "All Buddhas are entirely equal;

however, there are many whose faculties are dull, turbid, and distracted. If one does not single-mindedly fix one's mindfulness upon a single Buddha, the mind will become scattered and samādhi will be difficult to achieve.
Therefore, it specifically directs one to be mindful of Amitābha Buddha; this is precisely the 'one-mark' samādhi."

[The *Mèi* (Abridged) version states: The *Ratnarāja-śāstra* says: "One who practices the single-character *nien-fo samādhi* should maintain mindfulness without forgetting while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down.
Even when falling into deep sleep, one should continue to maintain mindfulness while sleeping; upon waking, one should resume it immediately.

One must not allow other activities to interrupt it, nor allow greed, anger, and the like to create a gap between moments. One should repent immediately upon committing a transgression, without allowing even a single thought-moment to intervene or to diverge."

Contemplate thus: without a day’s interval and without a moment’s interval, at every thought-moment you are never separated from the Buddha; at every thought-moment you are pure, perfect, and luminous.
This is precisely the attainment of the Samādhi of the Single Characteristic.
All those who practice the Pure Land path must resolutely confront birth and death; it is not a matter of merely speaking of it and then leaving it at that.
One should reflect upon how impermanence is swift and how time does not wait for anyone; one must treat this as a single, paramount task.

If one advances only half-heartedly and retreats just as often, or if one wavers between faith and doubt, what possible benefit will there be when the end comes? How can such a person escape [the cycle]?
One departs from saṃsāra. If you can gain such conviction, then from this very day forth, arouse great courage and great diligence.
Do not concern yourself with whether you understand or not, nor whether you have seen your nature or not;
simply hold fast to the single phrase, "Namo Amitābha Buddha," as if leaning against Mount Sumeru, unshakable and immovable, focusing your mind exclusively upon it.

Focus the mind and unify its intent. Whether through contemplation, reflection, mindfulness, or ten recitations; whether through silent recitation, single-minded recitation, focused recitation, or reverent recitation—let the thought remain here, right here.
Constantly remember, constantly recite. Recite at dawn and recite at dusk; recite while sitting and recite while walking. Let the mind not pass by in vain;
let the recitation of the Buddha never depart from the heart. Day after day, moment after moment, do not abandon it.
Continuous and dense, like a hen brooding her eggs, one must constantly ensure that the warmth remains uninterrupted; this is precisely what it means for pure mindfulness to succeed one another.
When further augmented by the illumination of wisdom, one realizes that the Pure Land is none other than one’s own mind. This is the method of cultivation for those of superior intelligence.

Having thus attained stability in their embrace, mastery in their practice, and firmness in their reliance, they remain unshaken even when encountering circumstances of suffering or joy, adversity or favor.

Manifestly present before you, simply recite the name of Amitābha Buddha. Do not harbor a single thought of wavering mind, do not harbor a single thought of indolence, and do not harbor a single thought of distracted conceptualization.
Continue until the end of this life, never entertaining another thought, with the resolute determination to be born in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.
If one can apply oneself with such diligence, then the ignorance accumulated over kalpas and the karmic obstacles of birth and death—

Defilements and habitual outflows will naturally dissolve and perish; they will naturally be purified and exhausted without remainder. One will behold Amitābha face-to-face, never departing from the original mindfulness.
When merit is perfected and practice fulfilled, supported by the power of one's vows, at the moment of death, one will certainly be reborn in the highest grade.
If a person who practices mindfulness of the Buddha has not yet purified their defilements and evil thoughts arise, they must examine themselves.

Perhaps there is a mind of stinginess and greed, a mind of anger and resentment, a mind of deluded attachment, a mind of jealousy, a mind of deceit and fraud, a mind of "I" and "mine," or a mind of arrogance.

When a mind of flattery and crookedness, a mind of false views, a mind of arrogance, a mind of subject and object, or a mind that converses with favorable or adverse conditions—indeed, any unwholesome mind arising through the influence of defilements—should arise, one must immediately call upon the Buddha’s name with a loud voice, collect the mind, and return to correctness.
Do not allow these evil thoughts to continue; straightaway strike them down until they are completely purified, so that they never arise again. All...
One should constantly protect and maintain the mind of deep faith, the mind of utmost sincerity, the mind of making vows and dedication,
the mind of compassion, the mind of humility, the mind of equanimity, the mind of skillful means, the mind of patience, the mind of upholding the precepts, the mind of joyful relinquishment,

the mind of meditative concentration, the mind of diligence, the mind of bodhicitta, and all other wholesome minds. Furthermore, one must distance oneself from unchaste conduct and sever all evil disciplines.
One must be careful never to keep chickens, dogs, pigs, or sheep as livestock. Hunting, trapping, and fishing are all activities that should not be undertaken.

One should know that the many superior virtuous persons within the land of Ultimate Bliss have attained rebirth in that Pure Land precisely because they abandoned evil conditions and followed the practice of wholesome deeds.
One shall not regress from Bodhi. Those who practice the mindfulness of the Buddha should follow the Buddha’s example and take the avoidance of evil and the adoption of good as their guiding precept.

Generally, those who cultivate the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha and desire to be born in the Pure Land should constantly reflect upon the impermanence of all things in this world; for once formed, [they must inevitably perish].

There is decay; birth is inevitably followed by death. If one does not personally hear the Buddha’s Dharma, then upon casting off this body and receiving another, one will transmigrate through the three realms, the four modes of birth, and the six paths of existence, with no prospect of liberation.
Now, having the necessary conditions, I have been able to hear the True Dharma and cultivate pure karma.
With the Buddha alone as my object of mindfulness, when I cast off this retribution-body, I shall be born in the Pure Land, enter that lotus-womb, and experience all manner of bliss.
Joyfully and eternally liberated from birth and death, never regressing from Bodhi—this is the lifelong accomplishment of a great man.
Should illness arise, it is precisely at this time that one must advance with a broad and open mind and body; do not harbor doubts or suspicions.
One must simply sit facing west in the correct posture, single-mindedly visualizing Amitābha Buddha, along with Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattvas, and countless others.
A transformation Buddha will appear before you. Recite "Namo Amitābha Buddha" with single-minded devotion, without a single sound ceasing.
Regarding all worldly affairs, you must not think of them nor harbor any attachment.

Should thoughts of them arise, you must immediately recite the Buddha’s name. In every moment of mindfulness, your karmic obstacles and hindrances shall be extinguished. If the patient falls into a stupor...
If one becomes exhausted and is unable to maintain mindfulness on one's own, the caregiver should employ skillful means to exhort and instruct them.

By applying the mind in this way, they assist the dying person until their life comes to an end; by this single thought alone, rebirth in the Pure Land is assured. Should their life not yet have ended, [the same applies].
You shall naturally attain peace and security. Be careful not to give rise to thoughts of attachment to this world.

You must live as you live; you must die when it is time to die. Simply prepare for rebirth—why harbor doubts? If you understand this principle, it is like casting off worn-out clothes to don new garments.
Once you abandon this ordinary body, you will immediately ascend to the stage of Buddhahood. How marvelous! How magnificent! It is ultimate; it is complete.
A practitioner who possesses true faith must, with absolute sincerity, be reborn in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.
With single-minded focus on a single thought, they should hold the name of Amitābha Buddha. This single thought alone is my original teacher; this single thought alone is...
This is precisely the transformation Buddha. This single thought-moment is the valiant general who shatters the hells;
this single thought-moment is the precious sword that slays the multitudes of evil; this single thought-moment is the bright lamp that opens up the darkness;
this single thought-moment is the great ship that ferries one across the sea of suffering; this single thought-moment is the excellent remedy for escaping birth and death. This...
This single thought-moment is the path for exiting the triple world. This very thought-moment is the Original Nature Amitābha.
This very thought-moment reaches the Pure Land of Mind-Only. It is sufficient simply to remember this one phrase, "Amitābha Buddha," and keep it in mind without letting it be lost.
Let every thought-moment constantly manifest before you; let every thought-moment never depart from the mind. Even when there is nothing to do, it is thus.
This is mindfulness. One is mindful of matters in this way; one is mindful of peace and happiness in this way; one is mindful of the suffering of illness in this way;
one is mindful of birth in this way; and one is mindful of death in this way.
When such a single thought is clear and undimmed, why even need to ask others for the path home?
Regarding the Pure Land, one might ask:

Master Tianru said that if one has committed evil throughout their life but recites the Buddha’s name at the moment of death, they will be reborn there while still carrying their karmic burdens, and furthermore, they will not fall back.
This power of Amitābha’s vows is truly inconceivable. Nevertheless, while alive, I shall first attend to my worldly affairs...
"Regarding the practice of one's vocation: is it permissible to wait until the very moment of death before practicing *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation)?

He replied, "Alas, alas! What kind of foolish and erroneous words are these? Arsenic and poisoned wine are the most lethal of poisons; yet your current words are more poisonous than arsenic and poisoned wine.
Not only do they deceive and mislead yourself, but they also deceive and mislead all those in the world, whether they be monks or [laypeople]."
The "laymen and laywomen who are virtuous" refers precisely to this.

As for those previously mentioned—ordinary, evil people who encounter the Buddha at the moment of death—it is because they possess roots of goodness and the karmic conditions of merit from former lives that they meet a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) and are thus able to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
Such fortunate occurrences happen not once in ten thousand people, nor even once in a hundred thousand; you should not assume that everyone will have this opportunity at the time of their death.

How fortunate this is! Do you not see what the *Qunyi lun* (Treatise on Resolving Doubts) says? "In the world, there are ten kinds of people who, at the time of death, are unable to practice the recitation of the Buddha's name:
first, they may not encounter a virtuous friend, and thus lack the opportunity for exhortation to recite;

second, their bodies are entangled by the suffering of karma, leaving them no leisure to recite the Buddha's name; third, they may suffer from a stroke that causes loss of speech, rendering them unable to invoke the Buddha's name; fourth..."
1. One’s mind becomes deranged and lost; focused contemplation cannot be accomplished. 2. Fifth, one may encounter water or fire, leaving no leisure for sincere practice.
3. Sixth, one may encounter jackals or wolves, finding no more virtuous friends. 4. Seventh, at the time of death, evil associates destroy one’s faith.
5. Eighth, by overeating to excess, one falls into a stupor and dies. 6. Ninth, in the midst of military arrays and battle, one suddenly perishes. 7. Tenth...
Suddenly falling from a high cliff and losing one's life—these ten kinds of matters are all things commonly heard of and seen with the eyes.
Whether monastic or lay, male or female, everyone encounters them. They may be summoned by past karma or induced by present karma;
they suddenly manifest before one, leaving no room for avoidance. You, moreover, are not a sage possessed of supernatural powers who has [transcended] past...

The faculty of the life-span (*āyus-saṃskāra*) allows one to know whether there is karma remaining at the moment of death or not; yet this is not the same as possessing the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) or the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*).
One can thus know whether the death will be auspicious or miserable. If any one of the ten kinds of evil conditions mentioned above suddenly befalls you, it is all over;
you will have no time to act or maneuver. Even if you are surrounded by learned teachers or living Buddhas, they cannot save you.
It is truly dire. One must inevitably undergo retribution according to one’s karma, suffering pain and incurring guilt within the three miserable realms and the eight difficult conditions.
By that time, it will be impossible even to hear the name of the Buddha.

Even if you were to avoid such evil conditions and merely die of a common illness, you would still not escape the wind-blades severing your limbs and the separation of the four elements, like a live turtle withdrawing from its shell.
When a crab falls into boiling water, it is oppressed by agony; terrified and frantic, it is unable to recite the Buddha’s name.

Even if you were to die without illness, or if your worldly affairs remain unfinished and your attachments to this world have not ceased—your mind agitated by the craving for life and the fear of death—and if you are a layperson, moreover, with your private family affairs unresolved and your posthumous matters unattended, while your wife weeps and your children...
Weeping, one is tormented by a hundred kinds of anxieties; one cannot bring oneself to recite the Buddha’s name.

Furthermore, even before you have died, when there is merely some slight illness upon your body, you endure it all, you suffer through it, you cry out and groan, you ask for medicine and seek out physicians, you pray and repent, and your distracted thoughts fly about;
you cannot bring yourself to recite the Buddha’s name. Furthermore, even before you have fallen ill...

This person is now advanced in years; the signs of decay appear before them. Exhausted and frail, they are burdened by grief, lamentation, and distress, merely struggling to arrange their limbs on this aging body until they can no longer recite the Buddha’s name.

Furthermore, even when you were not yet old—during the days of your youth and vigor—it was precisely the time to recite the Buddha’s name. Yet, if your wild mind had not yet been stilled, or if you were distracted by worldly...

Preoccupied with worldly affairs, you climb here and dangle there, lost in random thoughts; your karmic consciousness is vast and murky, and even if you practice the recitation of the Buddha's name, it will not suffice.

Furthermore, even if you are free from busyness and at ease, and possess the resolve to cultivate the Way, if you cannot penetrate through the appearances of the world, cannot let go of them, cannot hold them steady, and cannot remain seated amidst them, then suddenly some slight state of experience will manifest before you. One...
The master follows after such delusions; he is unable to practice the Buddha-mindfulness. Observe him when he is old and sick, and compare it to his days when he was young and at leisure:
if even a single matter hangs upon his mind, he is already unable to practice mindfulness—how much more so when facing the time of death?
Furthermore, for you to say, "I will attend to worldly affairs first," you are truly a fool. To speak thus is the talk of a fool.
I say this: I dare say you have misapplied your body and mind. Furthermore, worldly affairs are like dreams and illusions, like shadows and echoes;
which one among them has real efficacy? Which one can substitute for birth and death?

Even if you were to extensively build monasteries, increase the permanent endowments, strive for titles and rank, and cultivate connections with officials and the wealthy—do you think these constitute doing much good?

This is a matter of fact. Little do they realize that by doing so, they violate the Tathāgata’s precepts against failing to embody the fundamental source of the Way and against extensively constructing monasteries and temples.
Have you not heard it said that the achievements of conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*) harbor many faults? Before the heavenly realm is attained, the hells are already established;

before the nature of birth and death is clarified, all such acts become the root of suffering. Only when the light of the eyes falls to the ground at the time of undergoing suffering will one finally realize what was done throughout one's life.
This is entirely adding shackles to shackles, adding locks to locks; it is adding firewood and charcoal to the boiling cauldron, and assisting the swords and spears upon the sword-trees.
Under the *kāṣāya*, one loses their human form, and for ten thousand kalpas it will be difficult to regain. Even an iron-hearted man would have to shed tears upon hearing this.
When the Patriarch thus exhorted people with such bitter words, did he ever permit you to merely pursue worldly affairs, waiting until the moment of death?
Do you recite the Buddha’s name? Furthermore, have you not seen how Master Sīxīn said:

"The people of this world possess wealth and treasures as vast as mountains, with wives and concubines before them, enjoying themselves day and night. Do they not also desire to live forever in this world? Yet, alas, their future path is limited; it presses them from within the shadows.
When the tally arrives, it must be executed; there is no room for lingering or delay. The Old Man Yama does not yield to human wishes."
How can you remain unmoved? What face does the King of Ghosts have? Consider what you have personally seen with your own eyes and heard with your own ears:
in the streets before and the alleys behind, how many relatives, kinsmen, friends, brothers, and sturdy young men have died?
The people of the world often say, "I will wait until old age to recite the Buddha's name. Let me tell you this: on the road to the Yellow Springs, there is no such thing as waiting for old age.
Among the old and the young, how many can wait until they reach old age? Many die prematurely in their youth. Thus, with such a death-mind, I have spoken these bitter words to exhort you:
did I ever promise you that you might continue your worldly affairs and only then recite the Buddha’s name when facing the end?

You should reflect that there is but a brief time for a person to live in this world; it passes in the blink of an eye, like a spark on stone or a flash of lightning. Seize this while it is not yet too late.
Before old age and illness strike, shake off the body and mind and cast aside worldly affairs.
Seize every moment of daylight to recite the Buddha’s name; devote every hour of effort to cultivating pure karma.
Thus, when the time of death arrives—whether it be a "good death" or a "bad death"—my provisions for the journey will have been prepared in advance, and my path ahead will be secure and certain.
It is so. If you do not act accordingly, it will be difficult to remedy your regrets later. Reflect on this, reflect deeply!

Question: Regarding what was said above about shaking off the body and mind and casting aside worldly affairs, those caught in the nets of this world who occasionally find their circumstances favorable and their bodies and minds at ease may follow this practice. However, as for those whose worldly affairs are not...
If one were to dismiss [the practice], how then should they be instructed? The answer is:

For those caught within the net of the world who feel a profound sense of impermanence and apply themselves with sincere earnestness—regardless of whether it be suffering or pleasure, adversity or favor, stillness or bustle, leisure or haste—they may freely attend to public or private affairs, welcome guests, and attend to visitors;
even amidst the confusion of myriad conditions and the need to respond to challenges from all directions, their recitation of the Buddha’s name remains concurrent with these activities.
They do not obstruct one another. As the ancients said: "In the morning it is Amitābha; in the evening it is Amitābha.

Even if one is as busy as an arrow, one does not depart from Amitābha. It is also said: "Though the bamboo is dense, it does not hinder the flowing stream; though the mountain is high, how could it obstruct the flying white clouds?
For those whose worldly attachments are somewhat heavy and whose spiritual power is somewhat slight, they must likewise steal [moments of practice] amidst their busyness.
In leisure, seek stillness amidst the bustle. Each day, one should establish a daily practice by reciting either thirty thousand, ten thousand, three thousand, or one thousand times;
this must not be neglected for even a single day. Furthermore, for those who are extremely busy and have no moment of leisure, they must perform at least ten recitations every morning.
Through long-term cultivation, success will be achieved, and these efforts will not be in vain. Recite the Buddha’s name.
Beyond these, one may recite sutras and prostrate before the Buddha, perform repentance and make vows, cultivate various karmic connections, and perform various meritorious deeds.
According to one's capacity, one should practice giving and cultivate all manner of wholesome merits to assist [the practice]. Every iota of goodness must be dedicated toward the Western Land.
By applying effort in this way, not only will rebirth there be certain, but one’s spiritual rank will also be elevated.

Question: You have spoken generally of "mindfulness of the Buddha," yet you have not yet provided the specific method. Furthermore, the practice of the ten recitations and the dedication of merit remains unclear to me.
I would be grateful for a detailed explanation. Answer: Regarding mindfulness of the Buddha:

some practitioners focus exclusively on the thirty-two marks [of a Buddha], binding their minds to achieve meditative concentration (*samādhi*), such that whether their eyes are open or closed, they constantly behold the Buddha. Others simply and exclusively recite the name, maintaining it without distraction.
One may also attain the vision of the Buddha in this very body. In this context, for those who seek such a vision, it is generally superior to recite the Buddha’s name.

Regarding the method of reciting the Buddha’s name, one must restrain the mind so that it does not become distracted, maintaining a continuous flow of mindfulness and binding the object of focus to the Buddha’s name.
With every sound from the mouth, call upon Amitābha Buddha. Let the mind follow along with each syllable, making every word distinct and clear.
When reciting the Buddha’s name, regardless of the number of times, one must always maintain single-mindedness and a focused intent, with each thought succeeding the next in an unbroken continuity.

Only by doing so can a single thought-moment extinguish the sins of eighty billion kalpas of birth and death. If it is otherwise, it will be difficult to extinguish those sins. [This is] the ten recitations.
Every morning at dawn, face west, stand upright, and join your palms. Recite the name of Amitābha Buddha with a continuous voice;

one full breath constitutes one recitation (*nien*). Ten such breaths are called ten recitations (*shinian*). Simply follow the length of the breaths without concern for the number of repetitions of the Buddha’s name;

the only requirement is that they be long and sustained, with the breath reaching its limit as the measure. The sound of the Buddha’s name should be neither too high nor too low, and neither too slow nor too hurried.

It is not urgent; one should maintain a balanced moderation. In this way, ten breaths are connected in an uninterrupted succession. The intent is to prevent the mind from scattering, making single-minded diligence the primary practice.
Therefore, it is called "ten recitations" (*shiniàn*) to manifest that the mind is bound by means of the breath.

Throughout this entire life, one must not abandon this for even a single day. Regarding the dedication of merit and the making of vows: once the recitation of the Buddha’s name is completed, one immediately recites one...

The Text for Taking Refuge in Mind: Regarding the aforementioned methods of reciting the Buddha’s name, as for the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), it is a vital instruction bequeathed by the masters of old that has been widely disseminated in the world for a long time; one should follow and put it into practice.
Question: The contemplation of perfect cultivation and the mindfulness of the mind-only seem to be the practice-gates for those of superior capacity.

The ten vows of the *Avataṃsaka* and the ten minds of the *Ratnakūṭa* are likewise the functional application of those with great roots. If one’s faculties and vessel do not correspond to these, then such practices will be difficult to accomplish.
Now, when I examine my own faculties and observe what I prefer, it lies solely in the single-minded holding of the Name.
"When you have leisure, you simply add prostrations and repentance; what do you think of this? He replied, "Excellent, excellent!
You know your measure. Observing your words, they perfectly accord with the teaching of Shandao on exclusive and uninterrupted practice."

Regarding those who practice with single-minded devotion: precisely because it is easy to invoke the Name, the visualization arises in continuous succession. Regarding those who practice without interruption:
the body must exclusively prostrate to Amitābha Buddha, without mixing in other prostrations; the mouth must exclusively recite the name of Amitābha Buddha, without reciting other names or sutras;
the mind must exclusively contemplate Amitābha Buddha, without mixing in other thoughts. Furthermore, if one is greedy...
If anger or delusion should intervene, one should repent immediately upon committing the transgression, not allowing it to persist for even a day or a night, thereby constantly maintaining purity;
this is also called "uninterrupted cultivation."
Question: Is not the cultivation of continuous, moment-to-moment succession what I desire? Yet, alas, my power of concentration (*samādhi*) is not yet perfected, and my thoughts have no master.
In the mere blink of an eye, they have traveled a thousand or ten thousand miles away.

Furthermore, whenever I am obstructed by even a hair’s breadth of worldly affairs, I am unable to extricate myself for five days, ten days, half a month, or even a full month. What strategy should I employ?
[The Master] said, "Treat it with this. He replied, "Alas! This is a common affliction among scholars throughout the world.

When you are interrupted by such thoughts, if you do not apply the whip of diligent effort with great intensity, then even if you cultivate uninterrupted mindfulness, there will never be a time of achievement.
I have heard that the ancients had three methods of 'painful whipping'; I shall now present them to you once more. First,"

First is repaying kindness; second is resolving one's will; third is seeking verification. Regarding the first, repaying kindness: having already cultivated the Pure Land, one should contemplate repaying kindness.
While the kindness of the Buddha and the kindness of the state need not be discussed here, consider for a moment the kindness of one’s parents in raising and nurturing one.
Is this not a profound kindness? Is it not the virtue of your teachers who brought you to completion? Is this not a profound virtue?
At the very beginning of your renunciation, you spoke of wishing to repay this profound kindness; later, while traveling on pilgrimage, you again spoke of wishing to repay this profound virtue.

For twenty or thirty years, you have left your hometown and turned your back on your wellspring, showing no concern at all for the hardships and sufferings of your parents and teachers. When your parents grew old and fell ill, you—

Furthermore, you did not look after them, and now that you have heard of their death, you still do not return. Perhaps they are currently undergoing punishment and suffering in the three miserable realms;
I hope you will rescue them, I hope you will deliver them. Yet you instead sever your mindfulness moment by moment, so that the Pure Land is not realized.
If the Pure Land is not realized, you cannot even save yourself—how then can you save others? Since you are unable to help one another, you are ungrateful.
This is contrary to righteousness. Such a person is a great filial impiety. The sutras state that the sin of filial impiety leads one to fall into hell;
thus, even a single moment of a heart that has severed [its roots of goodness] constitutes the karma for hell. Furthermore, they wear clothes without weaving and eat food without plowing.
Regarding the bedding and requisites in the monastic quarters, which you currently enjoy and use: you ought to diligently cultivate pure karma to repay the grace of the donors' offerings.
As the Patriarch said: "This was gathered by the donors from what they themselves had diminished for the sake of their wives and children.

If your eye of the Way is not yet clear, then even a drop of water or a thread of silk must be repaid by pulling the plow and dragging the harrow before you can be free. Yet you, instead, let your mindfulness be interrupted at every moment. [Pure...]

The land will not be perfected; the Pure Land will not be realized. There is a portion of retribution to be paid. Thus, a mind that is interrupted for even a single thought-moment is itself the karma of an animal.
Second, regarding the resolution of the will: if you study with single-minded cultivation, your resolve must be decisive.

You have spent your entire life practicing Chan, yet you have not attained awakening through Chan; when it comes to studying the teachings, you do not understand them either. Having fumbled until now, you must contemplate—
Before his head has even died, he wishes to speak a few words of Chan, write a few characters, and compose a few poems. His emotions are entangled at both ends;
his thoughts branch into four directions. The Patriarch said: "A thought tied by a hair’s breadth becomes the karmic cause for the three miserable realms."
If a fleeting emotion arises, one is fettered for ten thousand kalpas. You, however, lack determination in your resolve and harbor manifold thoughts.
Because of these manifold thoughts, you interrupt right mindfulness. Thus, a single moment of an interrupted mind is itself the karma that binds one to the three miserable realms.
Furthermore, when guarding the roots of the precepts, if your resolve is not determined, you may, through body and speech, pursue objects in every thought-moment.
According to the teachings, it would be better to pour molten copper into one’s mouth than to receive food and drink with a mouth that has broken the precepts;
it would be better to wrap one’s body in glowing iron than to receive clothing with a body that has broken the precepts.

How much more so when, due to a lack of strictness in the various precepts, the deviant mind moves recklessly, and because of this reckless movement, true cultivation is interrupted. Thus, within a single thought-moment—
To sever the mind—how could this be merely a matter of molten iron and boiling copper? Furthermore, one must eliminate hatred and attachment.

When one’s resolve is not firm, one fails to reflect upon oneself regarding empty fame and fleeting profit; thus, when fame and profit belong to oneself, greed and love arise, and when they belong to others, hatred and envy arise.
As the ancients said: "Those who crave fame and profit share the same destiny as the realm of ghosts; they pursue their desires."
Chasing after hatred, we enter the same fiery pit together. Yet you, because of this love and hatred, create interruptions in the Pure Land.

Thus, a single thought of interruption is itself the karma for the fiery pit of hungry ghosts. Third, regarding seeking verification: once you have studied the practice of exclusive cultivation, you should seek spiritual efficacy.
Now that your hair has turned white and your face is wrinkled, the signs of death are manifest before you; you know that your end is near.
How many more days remain? You must have the Buddha before you; you must see the Buddha immediately.
For instance, Master Yuan of Mount Lu saw the Buddha three times throughout his life. Furthermore, Master Huai-gan called upon the Buddha’s name and immediately obtained a vision of the Buddha.
Likewise, when Master Shao-kang chanted the Buddha’s name once, the assembly saw a Buddha fly out from his mouth.
If you chant the name of the Buddha ten times, ten Buddhas will fly forth from your mouth. Such miraculous responses are countless—ten thousand, a hundred thousand, even a million.

If your mind remains uninterrupted, it will not be difficult to see the Buddhas; if an interrupted thought arises, you will certainly not see them. Since you do not see the Buddhas, you lack the karmic affinity with them.
Lacking this affinity with the Buddhas, it is difficult to be born in the Pure Land. If you are not born in the Pure Land, you will inevitably fall into the realms of suffering.
The evil realms. Thus, a single moment of interrupted thought is itself the karma for the three miserable paths.

Regarding the three strategies mentioned above, you should lash yourself with remorse so that your mindfulness does not depart from the Buddha, and the Buddha does not depart from your mindfulness; in this way, the resonance between cause and response will be perfectly interfused.
One sees the Buddha manifest before one. Having seen the Buddha of the Land of Bliss, one then sees all Buddhas of the ten directions.

Having seen all Buddhas of the ten directions, one then sees the Buddha of one’s own original nature, the true and heavenly. Having seen the Buddha of one’s own original nature, the true and heavenly, one then attains the manifestation of great function.
Thereafter, one dedicates that compassionate vow to extensively transform all sentient beings; this is called the Pure Land.
Chan is also called the Pure Land of Chan. [The author] replies:

My younger brother’s practice is far-reaching, yet I, being unworthy, have studied Chan; I am unable to cause my parents to realize the great matter of birth and death and to accomplish their path of cultivation. This...

This is indeed cause for shame. Yet, upon privately observing these two elders, I fear they may not be vessels for the study of Chan. To administer medicine that does not correspond to the ailment is to cause the ailment by means of the medicine itself.
Therefore, when returning in the autumn of the Jiazi year, I once took the Dharma-gate of *xiannian* (mindfulness) as the excellent prescription for their specific condition and diagnosis.
Since then, as days have passed and months have changed, regarding their conduct, their relinquishing or grasping, and their diligence or indolence—up until the point of [their passing]...
Whether or not one will ultimately attain this power is something entirely beyond my knowledge. Now, fortunately, my elderly mother still lives, yet she is nearly seventy;

how much time remains in her final years? This is another matter that cannot fail to be mentioned once more. As for the method of focused mindfulness, it is not restricted by walking, standing, sitting, or reclining;
there is no need to utter sounds or expend breath. One should simply strive for utmost sincerity, silently contemplating and silently reciting, moment after moment.

Following one after another with an uninterrupted mind, how could one dare say that it is only in this present life that the physical eye can see the Buddha, or perceive his radiance, or receive the blessing of his hand upon one’s head?
Furthermore, why must these events necessarily occur at the moment of death?
This is a direct and swift Dharma-gate—most simple and essential, most efficacious and verified. If one succeeds in being born in the Pure Land, one shall see the Buddha and hear the Dharma.
Do not worry that the Great Matter will remain obscure, that the cycle of birth and death will not be resolved, or that the work of the Way will not be accomplished.

Should this not be so, one would live in vain and die in obscurity; how then could one hope to escape the realms of suffering? I urge you, my younger brother, to explain these matters in detail to my compassionate mother.
You must by no means allow mundane affairs to occupy her mind; rather, you must provide her with skillful means every morning and evening.

This enables one to focus the mind with single-minded intent. That upon which one relies is the "one point" (the single seed). It is like a torch for illuminating the night, or a boat for crossing the sea;
it must not be abandoned for even a moment. If one can truly prepare such a practice in this way, one's efforts will never be in vain.
Thus, your filial piety in serving your parents could not be greater than this.
As for my mother, she was unable to find a foothold in the Chan school’s Way of Direct Pointing.

In the past, I once exhorted her to practice the Buddha-recitation with diligence, telling her that she should illuminate and see through the world as being entirely but a single dream-event; suffering is a dream, and joy is also a dream.
A dream. Wealth is a dream; poverty is also a dream. Do not be deluded by these dream-states.

To give rise to thoughts and create karma will lead you to waste your entire life, as you drift toward the three miserable realms of suffering. The suffering one undergoes in this present life is beyond description.
At such a time, your father and mother cannot save you; your children and grandchildren cannot take your place. Raise [your head]!
Look at this clearly: who can you rely upon? Only the Buddha of the Land of Bliss can deliver you, can take you into his care, can protect the Dharma, and can bring you to fulfillment.
You must, by all means, while your sight is clear and your feet are strong, place your entire being in reliance upon him.
Seek his compassion and mercy; pray with earnestness day and night, never for a moment letting go. If you do not rely upon him—
Steadfast! One cannot help but easily let this slip away; once regret sets in, it is difficult to pursue.

You should reflect that the remainder of your life is like dew upon the grass, a bubble upon the water, a candle in the wind, or fire within a stone—subject to change and impermanence, passing from morning to evening without delay.
You must not fail to apply yourself with urgency. This matter is not something only my mother can practice; all who see and hear of it should likewise encourage one another.
To offer exhortations and encourage one another to resolve to attain enlightenment is itself a form of great expedient means.

If you, my younger brother, will deeply discern my heart and assist in carrying out my words, then our departure for the Land of Bliss is certain, and the reunion of mother, son, younger brother, and elder brother can be expected.
What need is there to dwell upon returning to our native villages?
To Layman Yuet-t’ing: Master Ch’u-shan.
The true mechanism beyond the phenomenal realm admits no approach or settlement. Beginners must necessarily rely upon provisional means—the "trap" and the "snare.
That which is called Amitābha Buddha in Sanskrit is translated here as "Buddha of Immeasurable Life"; this is awakening. Awakening is precisely one's own [nature].
The mind. The mind is the original Buddha-nature. Therefore, one who recites the Buddha’s name is reciting the Buddha of one's own mind;
there is no need to seek it externally. This is what the Great Master Mazu meant when he said, "This very mind is Buddha.
Some may ask: "If this very mind is Buddha, why bother to recite the Buddha’s name? It is precisely because people do not realize that their own minds are Buddha. For this reason—
Grasping at appearances and following after names, they give rise to deluded confusion and falsely perceive birth and death, perversely entering the stream of ignorance.

Therefore, the former sages laboriously bestowed skillful means, instructing them to focus their thoughts and contemplate the mind. One must believe that one’s own mind is the Buddha; then one will know that recollecting the Buddha is recollecting the mind, and recollecting the mind is recollecting the Buddha.
With mindfulness unceasing and thought following upon thought without interval, suddenly one reaches the point where thought is no longer thought.

At the point where the path is cut off, the faculties and their objects are suddenly and completely liberated; the very substance is empty and still. Only then does one know that there is no thought and no mind.
When both mind and thought are absent, even the Buddha cannot be apprehended. Thus it is said: "From having thought, one arrives at no-thought;
by means of no-thought, one realizes the no-mind. This mind of no-mind is, for the first time, the true mind. No-thought...
Only when one is mindful can it be called right mindfulness. A Buddha who is no-Buddha may indeed be called Amitābha Buddha.
Upon reaching this state, not even a hair’s breadth of the marks of self and other can be found; how, then, could there be such things as sage and ordinary person, or delusion and awakening?
This very state of unfindability is the essential gateway for recognizing the mind and attaining the source, and the swift path for transcending birth and escaping death.

If a lay practitioner is indeed able to penetrate thoroughly to the very source and bottom of their own mind, they will finally believe that this ordinary dwelling in a burning house is itself the Western Land of Peaceful Nurturing;
that every step taken and every movement of the feet is nothing other than the site of the ancient Buddhas’ enlightenment;

and that the mountain streams and landscape colors manifest, point by point, the countenance of purple-golden skin, while the resonances of the valleys and the sounds of the wind unfold, one by one, the appearance of the red-lotus tongue. Thus, in every particle of dust, they accord with the wondrous.
Phenomenon after phenomenon embodies the essence, neither identical nor separate; mind after mind is liberated.
If you grasp this intent, you will surely smile with no doubt remaining. Layman, you must continue to exert yourself!
The "Buddha-Recitation Exhortation" by Chan Master Guyu:
"One Phrase Amitābha Buddha. This is the primary koan of the Zen school, like a staff held while riding a horse—a secure foundation for one's entire life.
It is not restricted to the four classes of practitioners; whoever maintains it will experience its efficacy throughout walking, standing, sitting, and lying down.

Within this, do not let even a single thought of Amitābha be interrupted. You must cultivate a profound cause so that the fruit may be profound; you must reach the point where he is remembered spontaneously without deliberate effort.

If you can ensure that every thought-moment is not empty, it is certain that your recitation will become a single, unified whole. While reciting, recognize the one who is reciting; then Amitābha and you will appear as one.
Thus you enter the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation and personally realize the inner court of Sukhāvatī, reaching the very goal of the lotus womb.

As for one's name, those who have attained ultimate merit will see it for themselves; they shall personally behold Amitābha bestowing upon them the prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa), and immediately become companions to the Bodhisattvas.
From this point on, they depart from the Sahā world, traveling a path entirely free of sorrow and affliction until reaching unsurpassed Bodhi.
For eternal kalpas, they may roam at ease according to their hearts' desire. Having returned by relying upon this Way, they are certain to attain Buddhahood without deficiency.
Answer: To Chancellor Dong of Huzhou and Master Lianchi:

The mind is fundamentally unborn; it arises through the convergence of conditions. The mind is fundamentally undying; it dies when conditions disperse. Thus, there is the appearance of birth and death.
Fundamentally, there is no coming or going; realize this within yourself. Then you will be at ease in life and peaceful in death, eternally tranquil and eternally luminous.
If you are as yet unable to do so, you should simply let go of everything completely and silently and continuously recite the single phrase "Namu Amida Butsu," seeking rebirth in the Pure Land.
Even if all conditions have not yet exhausted and one's lifespan has not ended, one should redouble one’s mindfulness of the Buddha; this brings great benefit.
The ancients said that the Dharma-gate of mindfulness of the Buddha is the longevity of the Golden Immortal.
In response to Zhang Baihu Guangtian: Deluded thoughts are the illness;
reciting the Buddha’s name is the medicine. A chronic illness cannot be cured by a single dose, and accumulated delusions cannot be eliminated by a momentary thought.
The principle is one and the same: do not concern yourself with the flight of deluded thoughts; it is simply a matter of valuing the recitation of the Buddha’s name.

It must be precise and incisive; every word must be distinct, and every sentence must follow seamlessly upon the last. Only by maintaining this with utmost diligence can one truly progress toward the goal.

As it is said, through "true accumulation and long-term effort," there comes a sudden, expansive realization—just as the metaphor of grinding a pestle into a needle or forging iron into steel is certainly not false.
There are many gates to entering the Way, but this single gate is the most direct shortcut; it must not be neglected.
One must not treat this with negligence.

Previously, I specifically exhorted the lay practitioner Liu of Suzhou through a letter to focus on *nianfo* (mindfulness of the Buddha) to seek rebirth in the Pure Land. Indeed, this path is most ultimate and most wondrous. Furthermore...
Furthermore, it is most simple and easy. Because it is so simple and easy, those of lofty intelligence overlook it. Indeed, birth and death do not depart from a single thought-moment;
even all the myriad phenomena of the mundane and supramundane worlds do not depart from a single thought-moment.

Now, by using this very thought-moment to recite the Buddha’s name, how intimate, immediate, refined, and substantial it is! If one can discern the place where this thought arises, that is the Amitābha of one's own nature.
This is precisely the intent of the Patriarch’s coming from the West. Even if you do not awaken, by relying on the power of this mindfulness, you will be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss;
you will thus crosscut the stream of birth and death and no longer undergo saṃsāra, for in the end, you shall surely attain great awakening.

I hope that you, O Elder, will let go of all worldly attachments and maintain mindfulness throughout the twelve periods of the day, constantly invoking and alerting your mind—this is my highest aspiration.
To the Layman Feng of Jiangyin, on his seventieth year, the age of "Ancient Rarity.

How few are the hundred years of life? Now, in these final years of one’s life, it is precisely appropriate to cast open the heart and mind and see through the world as being like a theatrical performance;
what therein has any true reality? Simply recite the name of Amitābha Buddha.
Pass the time in this manner, but regard only the Western World of Ultimate Bliss as your home.
As I now practice mindfulness of the Buddha, I shall surely be reborn in the West hereafter; how fortunate I am! Let great joy arise and do not give way to affliction.
Should you encounter circumstances that are unfavorable, immediately turn your mind around and swiftly recite the name of the Buddha. Then return [to your practice].
The light reflects back: "I am Amitābha Buddha. How can those within this world have the same limited perceptions as worldly people?
Turn your anger into joy and recite the Buddha’s name with single-minded devotion. This is the person of wisdom;
it is the Dharma-gate of great peace and great liberation.

The noble house of Wang, a *xiaolian* (honorable scholar) of Taicang, has cultivated magnificent virtue for generations. Why is it that your honored person has encountered such a severe illness? Could it not be that past karma has caused this to be so?
The causes of disease mostly stem from killing living beings; therefore, I have placed particular emphasis on the practice of releasing life. Now, furthermore—
I have something to submit. It is truly because the repentance performed by a monastic on one's behalf differs vastly in merit from the repentance performed within one's own mind.
I pray that you empty your mind, completely relinquish all external conditions, and within that state of emptiness, single-mindedly recite "Amitābha Buddha" just once.
What is called "mindfulness" does not necessarily require opening the mouth or moving the tongue; it simply means silently reflecting inwardly with the mind’s eye.
Each character must be distinct, each phrase continuous, from morning until evening and from evening until morning, with no interval between thought and thought.
If there is suffering, endure it and bear it, maintaining single-minded attention. As the Sutra says: "Mindfully recite the Buddha's name with utmost sincerity."
A single utterance extinguishes the grave offenses of birth and death accumulated over eight billion kalpas; thus, their merits are vastly different.
Answering the question of Guwang Yin:

For those who have already received the direct transmission of the Single Transmission from the ancients, yet later cultivate the practice of Pure Land and desire to be reborn there—how should they proceed?
Is this the practice that arises according to one's vows after awakening? Or is it the simultaneous cultivation of both practices before awakening?
If it is simultaneous cultivation, one falls into the path of a thieving mind and a divided mind; how then can one’s spiritual work become a solid mass?

If one has already awakened, then every dust mote is the Flower Treasury World and every location is a Lotus Land; there is nothing that is not permissible throughout the ten directions. Why then do you take pleasure solely in being reborn in the West?
Is this correct?
The answer is: For those who possess true faith in the Pure Land and are determined to attain rebirth there, it does not matter whether they have attained awakening or not.

Even for those who follow the "single transmission" and "direct pointing" [of Zen] but have not yet awakened—though their daily practice may consist solely of Chan meditation—it is not an obstacle to making the vow for rebirth in the Pure Land.
Because one has not yet attained non-acceptance of future existence and because there is still ultimately a place of birth, this is not a "thieving mind" nor a "diverging-path mind.
Regarding those who have already attained awakening, an ancient said: "Do you think that with a single awakening you can immediately rank as equal to all Buddhas?"

Therefore, Samantabhadra is the eldest son of the Avataṃsaka. Although every atom is a Flower Treasury and every location a Lotus Land, the "Chapter on Conduct and Vows" (Caryāpraṇidhāna-parivarta) invariably emphasizes with earnest devotion rebirth in Sukhāvatī.
This is true even for those who have already awakened; it can be known to be so for those who have not yet awakened.
Question: In the study of Chan, it is prized that not a single thought arises; in the recitation of the Buddha's name (*nienfo*), it is prized that pure mindfulness continues uninterrupted.
Now, regarding this method of investigating through the recitation of the Buddha’s name, the intent lies in attaining wondrous awakening and thereby achieving rebirth in the Pure Land.

Yet, at present, while the mind and the Buddha are distinct and clear during the time of recitation, both are completely severed during the time of investigation. Because they are severed, as the power of investigation gradually deepens, the force of recitation gradually diminishes. Thus—
How could there be both awakening and arising at another time? The answer is:
when not a single thought arises, this is Chan (meditation), not *can* (investigation). When thoughts arise and doubt descends, it is then called *can*. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:
"Furthermore, with this mind, investigate and examine back and forth," and so on. Both the moment of thought and the moment of *can* belong to the realm of having thoughts. Furthermore...
This is not contradictory.

When one asks about the principle that "mind itself is Buddha" and does not seek it externally, if one can believe it thoroughly and see it clearly, one may then simply follow conditions to exhaust past karma and refrain from creating new calamities.
Letting things proceed spontaneously and with ease, one awaits the natural drying up of consciousness.
Have you attained it? Or should you further give rise to a state of doubt, investigating with all your strength and striving for thorough inquiry in order to seek wondrous enlightenment?

The answer is: "The mind itself is Buddha. If you can truly believe this to its depths and see through it with complete penetration—reaching a state where everything is resolved and settled beyond a hundred doubts—only then may you proceed spontaneously through time. If this is not the case, you must not yet let go of your inquiry.

This shows that, in accordance with the teachings of the ancients, one should draw near to an enlightened teacher and seek out a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). Yet, such a spiritual friend truly possesses no secret dharma-gate transmitted orally or bestowed through the mind;
rather, simply untying the person's entanglements and removing their fetters is itself the secret. Now, you need only maintain this.
The eight characters "Recite the Name with single-mindedness without distraction" are themselves the secret dharma-gate for untying adhesions and casting off bonds;

they are the grand, open highway for escaping birth and death. Whether reciting in the morning or evening, while walking or sitting, let each thought follow the next in uninterrupted succession, and you will naturally achieve samādhi. Do not seek it elsewhere.
The essential gateway for warning the multitude to enter the Way is faith; it is the foremost. Even evil deeds do not succeed without faith, let alone virtuous ones.
For example, when worldly thieves are occasionally exposed, the government does not fail to punish them with the ultimate penalty; yet, as time passes—
Later he was released and pardoned, yet he remained as before without regret. Why was this? Because the other had gained confidence in this particular path;
without investing a single coin of capital, he personally reaped immeasurable profit. Therefore, even while undergoing all manner of suffering and pain, he was determined never to retreat or regret.

Nowadays, when people practice the recitation of the Buddha's name, they are unwilling to apply themselves with earnest diligence. This is simply because they have not reflected deeply or developed true faith.

It goes without saying that some do not believe in the Pure Land; however, even regarding a single phrase spoken by the World-Honored One—that "human life lies between a single inhalation and exhalation"—its meaning is not difficult to explain.
You have personally seen it with your own eyes and heard it with your own ears in the sutras.
I have cited many precedents. Now, I must ask you to believe these words; it will soon be too late.

If you truly believe these words, then regarding the method of reciting the Buddha’s name, there is no need for me to exhaust my strength in exhortations or to issue a thousand warnings and ten thousand instructions.
You will then proceed like water rushing into a ravine, such that even ten thousand oxen could not turn you back.
I have observed that when new students first grasp even a single phrase of the Buddha and place it upon their hearts, their idle thoughts and delusions become even more turbulent.
They then claim that the practice of *nianfo* (reciting the Buddha’s name) cannot still the mind.

They do not realize that the roots of birth and death accumulated over immeasurable kalpas—how could these be severed so suddenly? Furthermore, at the very moment when ten thousand thoughts are flying about, this is precisely the time to practice.
In the process of cultivation, as you gather, you scatter; as you scatter, you gather. After a long time, when your practice has become mature, delusive thoughts will naturally cease to arise.
Furthermore, your ability to perceive these delusive thoughts is nothing other than the functioning of the Buddha within you.
If it were not for this mindfulness of the Buddha, how could you possibly perceive those thoughts that surge like turbulent waves, ceasing not for even a single kṣaṇa?
In the practice of Buddha-recitation (*buddhānusmṛti*), there is silent recitation, there is loud recitation, and there is *vajra-holding* recitation.

Loud recitation may be felt to be too strenuous, while silent recitation may easily lead to dullness and sleepiness. Simply maintaining a continuous and dense flow, with the sound residing between the lips and teeth, is what is called *vajra-holding*.
Nevertheless, one must not remain fixed in this method; if it is felt to be strenuous, it is permissible to practice silent recitation. Or if [one feels...]
If you are drowsy, it is not improper to speak aloud. Those who recite the Buddha's name nowadays merely strike their hands like fish eggs while shouting along with their mouths;
for this reason, they fail to obtain benefit. You must ensure that every phrase leaves the mouth and enters the ear, and that every sound awakens your own mind.
It is like a person who is in a deep sleep; if another person calls out, "O [Name]," that person will immediately wake up. Thus it is said.
Because mindfulness of the Buddha can gather and stabilize the mind, people today are unwilling to practice it; they do so simply because they hold the Western Pure Land in contempt.

They fail to realize that rebirth in the West is the endeavor of those with great virtue, great merit, great wisdom, great insight, and who are truly sages and worthies—those capable of transforming this Sahā world into a pure land.
It is not a matter of some minor circumstance. You need only observe this city for a single day and night: how many people die?
Let alone being reborn in the Western Paradise, even among hundreds or thousands of people, there is not a single one who attains birth in the heavens.
As for those who pride themselves on their cultivation, they achieve nothing more than avoiding a fall into the human realm. Therefore, my World-Honored One, out of great compassion...

Alas! To reveal this Dharma gate is a merit that surpasses heaven and earth, an kindness exceeding that of one's own parents. Even to grind one's bones to powder and shatter one's body would be insufficient as a repayment.

Seng Haizhou came to pay his respects. The Master asked, "For what purpose have you left the household life? He replied, "I have left it to seek deliverance from suffering. The Master asked, "By what method do you seek deliverance from suffering?
He replied, "My faculties are dull; I simply recite the Buddha's name. The Master asked, "Is your recitation of the Buddha’s name constant or does it have interruptions?

He replied, "When I close my eyes and sleep, I forget it. The Master, manifesting a majestic aura, rebuked him, saying, "If you forget as soon as you close your eyes, how can you hope for deliverance?"
To practice mindfulness of the Buddha in this manner for ten thousand years would achieve nothing.
From this day forward, you must ensure that your mindfulness of the Buddha continues even within your dreams; only then will you have the possibility of escaping suffering.

If you cannot maintain mindfulness of the Buddha even in your dreams and forget it, then upon waking, you must weep aloud and go straight before the Buddha to prostrate until your head bleeds, or recite [the Buddha's name] a thousand times.

Recite the name [of the Buddha] ten thousand times, or as many times as your own strength permits, and then stop. Do this twenty or thirty times, and naturally, even amidst deep sleep, the Buddha will not cease to be present.
Furthermore, there are those in the world who recite the Buddha’s name for thirty or twenty years, or for the remainder of their lives;
yet when the time of death arrives, it is of no use. This is because they were merely sleeping.
This is because no thoughts arise within a dream. Human life is like waking, and human death is like dreaming.
Therefore, those who can bring the Buddha to mind while dreaming will naturally remain undisturbed at the moment of death.
The Dharma-door of mindfulness of the Buddha is the most simple and convenient. However, those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha today lack resolute determination;
therefore, though thousands or hundreds of people may recite the Buddha’s name, not even one or two among them achieve success.
This single phrase "Namo Amitābha Buddha" is that by which all Bodhisattvas, all devas, and all humans who are born in the Western Land do not fail to attain rebirth.
Amitābha Buddha delivers one across the sea of suffering. However, whether the mind of nianfo (recitation of the Buddha’s name) is genuine or not is a point to be scrutinized;
the very crux of this examination lies in taking proof from both states of joy and affliction. The distinction between a genuine and a false mind can be clearly discerned therein.
Generally speaking, for one who recites the Buddha’s name with a true mind, there will inevitably be no interruption in their mindfulness amidst both joy and affliction. Therefore—
Afflictions cannot move it; joy cannot move it. Since neither affliction nor joy can move it, one will naturally be free from fear and terror in the face of death and rebirth.
Nowadays, when people recite the Buddha's name, as soon as even a slight amount of joy or anger comes before them, Amitābha Buddha is cast behind their heads.
How then can they expect the spiritual efficacy of reciting the Buddha’s name? If one follows...

I am mindful of the Buddha. If you are unable to maintain this phrase "Amitābha Buddha" at the critical juncture between love and hatred, you will fail to enjoy its benefits in the present life and fail to attain rebirth at the time of death. My tongue-organ will surely wither and rot.
If you do not practice according to my instructions, then the lack of efficacy in your recitation of the Buddha's name rests entirely upon you; it has nothing to do with me.
At the beginning of the Jiajing era, about seven *li* behind Wan’gu Temple in Puzhou, there was a shrine called Zantan.

Within it lived an elderly monk named Yixiu, a native of Wenli, who was diligent and sincere. He recited the name of Amitābha Buddha more than one hundred thousand times daily, without ceasing morning or night for over fifty years.
Even at the place where he practiced walking meditation (*caṅkrama*), the path had been worn into a channel by his feet, as if paved with bricks. Or...
He wore them until they reached the soles. People tried to patch them, but after a long time they would become worn through again; they remain there even now.

Initially, there was a poor man who could not support himself, and he came to rely on Xiu. Xiu took him in, but after some time, seeing that his conduct was not good, he rebuked him, saying, "You are truly a thief.
Not long after, the man indeed conspired with his associates to attack Xiu at night. When they first struck him, Xiu called out the name of the Buddha.
