The sound was still loud. He struck again, and Xiu called out "Buddha," the voice not ceasing; yet it had already grown faint. Consequently, he died. Alas!
At the moment his life was about to end, the sound of "Buddha" did not cease. Even as his thigh broke, he was able to pass away in the full lotus posture.
Were it not for fifty years of firm and upright resolve, how could he have reached such a state?

Master Hanshan’s "The Essentiality of Mindfulness of the Buddha" and "Mindfulness of the Buddha for Rebirth in the Pure Land" were originally intended to resolve the great matter of birth and death; thus it is said, "Mindfulness of the Buddha resolves birth and death.
Nowadays, people only develop the aspiration to practice mindfulness of the Buddha because they wish to resolve the matter of birth and death. They merely speak of the Buddha...
This can bring an end to birth and death. If one does not know the root and trunk of birth and death, toward what, ultimately, will one direct one's mindfulness?
If the mind that recites the Buddha’s name cannot sever the root and trunk of birth and death, how can one bring them to an end?
What is the root and trunk of birth and death? An ancient said: "If karma is not heavy, one is not born in Saha; if craving is not severed, one is not born in the Pure Land."
Thus we know that the root of craving is the very trunk of birth and death.
Tracing this root of craving back, it was not acquired in this present life, nor was it acquired in one, two, three, or four lifetimes;

rather, from the very beginning of the commencement of birth and death in the infinite past, throughout every successive life and rebirth, one has undergone the cycle of transmigration through craving and desire, continuing right up to this day.
Reflecting back on the past, when has there ever been even a single thought that momentarily departed from this root of craving?

Such seeds of craving have accumulated over kalpas until they are profound and deep; therefore, birth and death are endless. Only today have you finally resolved to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, yet you merely hope in vain for rebirth in the Western Paradise.
You do not even know the name of this craving, which is the very root of birth and death—how could you have ever...?

There is a single thought-moment of attachment. Since one does not know the root of birth and death, one recites the Buddha’s name on one side while the root of birth and death continues to grow unchecked.
Reciting the Buddha’s name in this manner leaves it entirely unrelated to birth and death.
When the time of death arrives, one sees only the root of craving for life manifest before one; only then does one realize that the Buddha has provided no help at all, and one begins to resent Him.
If there is no spiritual efficacy in your mindfulness of the Buddha, it will be too late for regret. Therefore, I exhort those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha today:
first, you must understand that craving is the root of birth and death. As you practice mindfulness of the Buddha now, in every thought-moment you must sever this root of craving.
Even amidst daily activities, when practicing mindfulness at home, look upon children, grandchildren, family affairs, and property; not a single one of these [should be grasped].
If it is not love, then there is not a single matter or a single thought that is not the active pursuit of birth and death.
It is as if one’s entire body were within a pit of fire. One does not realize that while reciting the Buddha’s name, the root of attachment has never been set down for even a single moment.
Attachment is the sovereign; the recitation of the Buddha’s name is merely the surface. Thus, the Buddha hears only the recitation, while attachment remains...
Listen well. Furthermore, when the emotions of children and women manifest before you, turn the light inward and look at that one invocation of the Buddha’s name.
Is it truly able to withstand such love? Is it truly able to sever such love? If you cannot sever such love, how will you ever ultimately resolve the cycle of birth and death?
Because the conditions of love have been habituated through many lifetimes, as soon as you resolve to recite the Buddha’s name, [the obstacles arise].

This is superficial and lacks practical substance; therefore, it yields no power. If you cannot maintain firm resolve regarding the objects of attachment before your eyes, you will ultimately be unable to maintain it at the moment of death.
Thus, for those who joyfully recite the Buddha's name, the foremost requirement is to know that their resolve for liberation from birth and death must be urgent;
they must sever the urge for birth and death with urgency; and they must, at every thought-moment, apply themselves directly to the very root of birth and death.
To sever [delusion]—this is the moment of realizing birth-and-death in every thought-moment. When each thought is thus earnest and true, with every stroke of the blade one sees blood.
If one does not transcend birth-and-death, then all Buddhas would be guilty of speaking falsehoods.
Therefore, whether lay or ordained, if you simply understand the mind of birth-and-death, you will know the timing of transcending birth-and-death. How could there be any other wondrous dharma?
When the lay practitioner Jingxin went to visit the Old Man in Wuzhong, he paid his respects and requested instruction. The Old Man instructed him in the Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation (*nienfo*),
explaining that because the practice of Buddha-recitation is like a water-clearing pearl capable of purifying turbid water, one should take purity of mind as the Way.
It has been several years since we last met. Your recent letter states that you find it difficult to achieve single-mindedness in the practice of *nienfo*, and you again request my guidance.
In response, I have shown him this: "The foremost requirement for cultivation is an urgent sense of the reality of birth and death. If the urgency regarding birth and death is not present,"

How can one dare to claim that their recitation of the Buddha’s name has reached a state of "forming a solid mass"? Furthermore, since sentient beings have come from immeasurable kalpas ago, every thought has been a deluded fantasy, and their emotional faculties have remained firmly obscured.
Even though they have now entered this present life, they have never for a single moment felt a deep, urgent concern for birth and death.

Day after day, thought after thought, they follow their emotions and have never once turned back to reflect. Now, wishing to sever the cycle of birth and death accumulated over many kalpas by means of a superficial and floating faith—how could this possibly succeed?
To speak of using a drop of water to extinguish a fire of piled firewood—is such a principle even possible?

If one truly regards birth and death with urgency, and maintains a state of mind like that of someone whose hair is on fire, one will only fear that once this human body is lost, it will be difficult to regain it for a hundred kalpas.
One must bite down upon this single sound of "Buddha," resolutely confronting it at all times. It must manifest in every thought-moment, so that one is not overcome by delusive thoughts.
Delusive thoughts act as obstructions. Through such diligent and earnest effort over a long period, until one becomes thoroughly proficient, there will be spontaneous resonance.
Thus, without seeking to form a continuous state, it naturally becomes one. This matter is like a person drinking water; whether it is cold or warm, they know it for themselves.
It cannot be told to others; it depends entirely on one’s own exertion. If one merely takes the recitation of the Buddha's name as a mask...
Like a donkey’s hide, there will never be a time for its use; you must simply be courageous and not hesitate further.
Regarding these words on the Pure Land, Master Youxi said:
"If your love is not heavy, you will not be born in Saṃsāra; if your mindfulness is not single-minded, you will not be born in Sukhāvatī. Saṃsāra...
If one has even a single attachment that is not slight, at the moment of death one will be pulled by that attachment; how much more so when there are many attachments?
If there is even a single moment of mental distraction in the Pure Land, at the moment of death one will be turned by that thought; how much more so when there are many thoughts?
Now, attachments may be slight or heavy, thick or thin, pertaining to the primary retribution or the secondary environment. To enumerate their categories:
Parents, wives, and children; brothers and friends; fame, achievement, wealth, and honor; essays, prose, and poetry; arts, skills, and crafts;
clothing, food, and drink; houses, dwellings, fields, and gardens; forests, springs, flowers, and plants; and precious treasures and objects of play—these cannot be fully exhausted.
There is one thing that is never forgotten: it is love. There is one thought that is never lost: it is love. When there is a single love preserved within the breast, thoughts become manifold;
when there is a single thought that does not return to the One, life cannot be born. Someone asked, "Is there a way to diminish love?
He replied, "To diminish love, nothing is more essential than a single thought. He was further asked, "Is there a way for a single thought? He replied, "A single thought..."
Do not underestimate the power of attachment; it is because the mind lacks focus. This lack of focus arises from the mind being distracted by various objects.

Such distraction occurs because the mind chases after sensory realms, racing wildly outward. In this Sahā world, for every object there is a corresponding state of mind in sentient beings. Because each sentient being possesses such a mind, the Sahā world consists of a single realm of objects.
When the mind gathers its conditions within, it wavers; when it rushes toward external objects, it gallops away. Thus, the mind and its objects interact in mutual entanglement.
They rush about; their attachments are as numerous as dust motes in the sands. Therefore, if one wishes to diminish these attachments, there is nothing better than blocking off their objects.

When all objects are empty, the myriad conditions are entirely stilled. When the myriad conditions are entirely stilled, the single thought-moment is spontaneously perfected. If the single thought-moment is perfected, then both attachment and its conditions are exhausted.
He asked: "Is there a way to block off these objects? He replied: "To block off objects does not mean to eliminate the myriad existents, nor does it mean..."
Closing the eyes means not observing. This is to realize the emptiness of objects by confronting them directly, and to empty the branches by returning to the root.

All phenomena (*dharmas*) are fundamentally non-existent; their appearance as existent is due to the mind’s emotional attachments (*qing*). Thus, when attachment exists, objects exist; when attachment is empty, objects are empty.

When all phenomena are empty, the original nature manifests; when the original nature manifests, emotional thoughts cease. This occurs spontaneously and naturally, without the need for forced effort. (From the *Lengyan Sutra*)
What is meant by "strictness" is this: that which is called the seer and the objects of seeing, as well as the perceived characteristics, are like flowers in the sky—originally non-existent.
This seeing and its objects are, from the beginning, the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of bodhi. How could there be "is" or "is not" within them?

Therefore, to block off external objects, nothing is better than realizing the emptiness of things. When one realizes the emptiness of things, emotional attachments naturally cease; when attachments cease, [the mind is at peace].
Attachment does not arise from itself; it is merely a manifestation of the mind. Once this is realized, one becomes whole. Thus, the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* says:

"To know that things are illusory is to leave them; no expedient means are required. To leave illusion is to awaken; there is no gradual progression. There is neither going nor staying, and no room for wavering.
The efficacy is as swift as a drum struck by a mallet. Students of the Way should devote their full hearts to this. It is called: "Lightening Attachment."

"I have already heard your instructions. But what shall I do regarding this single thought? He replied, "The Way of the single thought has three aspects: faith, practice, and aspiration. To be free from doubt is called faith.
If there is even a slight doubt, the mind cannot attain singleness. Therefore, in seeking birth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, one must take the cultivation of faith as the beginning.
One must read the Mahāyāna scriptures thoroughly and study the ancestral teachings extensively; for it is these that reveal [the truth]."

Regarding the texts on the Pure Land, one must investigate each and every one of them. One must realize that the Land of Ultimate Bliss is originally the pure land of one's own mind and is not some other land;
and that Amitābha is originally the true Buddha of one's own fundamental nature and is not some other Buddha.
The essentials are twofold: first, awakening to the fact that wondrous existence is all-pervasive and fully endowed, taking this as the basis for delighting in purity;

second, awakening to the fact that true emptiness is perfectly detached and perfectly liberated, taking this as the source for relinquishing defilement. As for the second, the practitioner must cultivate firm faith, like seeing with one's own eyes.
Cultivation is like walking with one's feet. To have faith but not practice is like having eyes but no feet; to practice but lack faith is like having feet but no eyes.
Therefore, once both faith and understanding are complete, one should practice the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānusmṛti), just as when both eyes and feet are fully possessed.
One can reach the Cool Pond. There are two types of practice for entering this gate: the primary and the auxiliary. The primary practice is further divided into two:
invoking the name and visualization. Invoking the name is as described in the *Smaller Amitābha Sūtra*: reciting the name for seven days with single-mindedness and without distraction.

This consists of both the single-mindedness of phenomena and the single-mindedness of principle. If one invokes the Buddha’s name orally, binding the mind to that object so that the sounds follow one another in succession and the moments of consciousness [are likewise continuous].
Do not allow distraction. If the mind should happen to take external objects as its object, gather it back. This requires the generation of a resolute mind:
sever thoughts of the future, cast aside worldly affairs, and let go of the攀缘心 (clinging mind). Cause the mindful mind to grow gradually; from gradual to prolonged.
From few to many, for one day, two days, and even up to seven days, one must ultimately achieve single-mindedness without distraction before ceasing.
This matter is that of single-mindedness. If this is attained, then the pure cause for rebirth in Sukhāvatī is accomplished.
The right mindfulness at the moment of death will certainly be present; the body will be free from the suffering of illness, and one will not be entangled by evil states.

Knowing in advance that the time has come, one’s body and mind will be filled with joy, and one will pass away in auspiciousness—whether sitting or standing. One will see Amitābha Buddha face-to-face as he emits light to welcome and guide them, and birth in the Pure Land is certain.
The principle of single-mindedness is no different: it simply means that within the single mind of practice, one clearly realizes [the truth] in every thought-moment.
The mind capable of mindfulness and the Buddha who is the object of mindfulness are equal throughout the three periods of time and mutually interfused throughout the ten directions.

They are neither empty nor existent; neither self nor other; neither departing nor arriving; neither arising nor ceasing. This present single thought-moment is itself the boundary of the future Pure Land.
To mindfully recite while being beyond mindfulness, to be mindful while being without mindfulness, to arise while being without arising—this is true arising.
Yet there is no arising. Within that which is beyond thought, one intensely contemplates; within that which is unborn, one intensely seeks birth.

This is what is meant by "the single mind of phenomena" and "the single mind of clarity. Second, regarding the visualization: as fully described in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, there are sixteen objects of contemplation.
Contemplating the Buddha is most essential. One should visualize the six-foot body of Amitābha Buddha, creating [it]...
An image of purple-gold hue stands upon a lotus pond, making the gesture of extending a hand in invitation.

Its body possesses the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*), and each mark is adorned with eighty secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*). To form this visualization involves both the phenomenal and the principled aspects.
Phenomenally, one binds the mind to the Buddha and the Buddha to the mind. First, one contemplates the soles of the feet, which are level and even like the bottom of a casket.
Next, one contemplates the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel. Following this sequence, one traces the marks in reverse order up to the *uṣṇīṣa* (cranial protuberance) on the crown of the head.

Then, from the *uṣṇīṣa*, one traces them in forward order back down as far as the soles of the feet, perceiving them with perfect clarity and without any distraction. Regarding the principle of single-mindedness, the Sūtra says:
"The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are the body of the Dharma-realm; they enter into the thoughts and minds of all sentient beings. Therefore, the mind...
When one contemplates the Buddha, this very mind is the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics; this mind creates the Buddha, and this mind is the Buddha.
The ocean of the Tathāgatas’ perfect and universal knowledge arises from the mind’s contemplation. Therefore, you all should fix your mindfulness upon that Buddha.
This meaning fully elucidates the subtle and wondrous threefold contemplation, as explained in the *Miaozongchao* (Subtle Pivot Commentary) on the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*.
However, these two types of correct practice must proceed in mutual dependence. Whenever one is walking, standing, sleeping, or reclining, one should single-mindedly recite the Name.
Whenever one is sitting cross-legged, one should apply contemplation with every thought. When weary from walking, one should sit cross-legged to contemplate the Buddha;

when rising from sitting, one should perform walking meditation while reciting the Name. If one cultivates this without interruption throughout the four modes of deportment, one will be reborn in the Pure Land.
It is certain that these are the [true] lands. There are two types of auxiliary practices, which are also twofold:

first, worldly practices, such as being filial and obedient to one's parents, practicing worldly benevolence and compassion, maintaining a compassionate heart and refraining from killing, observing all the precepts, and performing all manner of beneficial deeds;

if these can be dedicated toward the Western Land, there is nothing among them that does not assist the path. Second, world-transcending practices, such as the six perfections and the myriad practices of cultivation.
When cultivating various merits, reciting Mahāyāna sutras, and practicing various methods of repentance, one must also assist these practices with a mind of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*);

there is nothing that is not a practice for the Pure Land. Furthermore, there is another subtle and wondrous auxiliary practice: whenever encountering conditions or objects, one should apply the mind in every situation.
For instance, when seeing one's kinsmen, one should regard them as spiritual kin of the Western Land, employing the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land.
Guide them in this way: cause their light affection to unify their thoughts, so that they may forever become non-arising kin in the future.
When feelings of attachment arise, one should contemplate the kin of the Pure Land; since there is no emotional craving there, when will I be able to be born in the Pure Land?
One must distance oneself from such attachment. When feelings of anger arise, one should contemplate the kin of the Pure Land, who are free from provocation and affliction; when will I...

Upon rebirth in the Pure Land, one shall be free from this anger. When experiencing suffering, one should contemplate that in the Pure Land there are no manifold sufferings, but only the reception of all manner of bliss.
When experiencing pleasure, one should contemplate that the bliss of the Pure Land is boundless and without dependence.
Whenever encountering circumstances or objects, one should expand upon this intention; thus, at all times and in all places, everything will be none other than the Pure Land.
This is the auxiliary practice. Regarding the third vow: the vessel for the Pure Land must take faith as its rudder, and practice as its oars, paddles, mast, and rigging;
the vow serves as the wind-sail. Without a rudder, there is no direction to follow; without oars, paddles, mast, and rigging, one cannot move forward;
and without a wind-sail, one cannot break through the waves to reach the destination swiftly. Therefore, the vow is explained immediately following practice.

Furthermore, there are distinctions of general and specific, broad and narrow, and universal and limited. "General" refers to the texts for dedication and aspiration established by ancient masters. "Specific" means following one's own intentions.
"Broad" refers to the Four Great Vows of seeking enlightenment above and transforming beings below. "Narrow" refers to making a resolution according to one's capacity to be reborn [in the Pure Land].
"Limited" refers to occasions such as formal recitation services where one joins the assembly to make the aspiration together. "Universal" means making the aspiration at all times.
As for making vows, one should direct the mind toward them in every instance; however, they must accord with the four great aspirations and must not be established through arbitrary self-opinion.
Generally speaking, specific vows are superior to general ones. General vows may follow the shifting words of others, whereas specific vows are directed by one’s own resolve.

Nevertheless, one should generate a firm determination based on the general texts, so that while being specific, one remains grounded in the general. If, however, one allows the specific texts to become muddled or diffuse, the specific [vows] will fail.

This also establishes universality. Furthermore, the broad surpasses the narrow; the broad involves a great resolve for enlightenment and yields superior results, whereas the narrow involves shallow compassion and vows, resulting in inferior attainment.
Moreover, the pervasive surpasses the limited; the limited is repeatedly interrupted, while the pervasive is perfected in every moment.
By means of these three dharmas, one may aspire to be born in the Pure Land and swiftly behold Amitābha. These are the dharmas of all pure lands.
The gateways [of practice] do not go beyond this.
Yuan Hongdao of the West was a practitioner of single-minded faith.
As the Sūtra says: "Faith is the source of the Way and the mother of merit; for all practices, faith is the..."
The primary cause: even until the fruit of Bodhi is perfected, one merely completes this faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).

It is like a grain seed fallen to the earth; when it finally bears fruit, it is no different from the original seed. Or like a young bamboo shoot reaching toward the heavens; its essence is originally that of the parent stalk.

There is not a single bodhisattva of initial resolve who does not achieve accomplishment by relying on the power of faith. In the Lotus School (*Lianzong*), faith is especially relied upon as the root. To believe once in Amitābha—
The fundamental wisdom of the Tathāgata’s immovable wisdom is no different from one's own self; it is like the great void of space: when the sun shines upon it, it is bright;
when clouds come, it is obscured. This is because the void is fundamentally non-existent, and furthermore, because the clouds and the sun are themselves the void.
Second, I am also able to practice the various forms of cultivation that were difficult to perform and difficult to endure for Amitābha Buddha over the course of *nayuta* kalpas.

One should practice. Why is this? Since beginningless time, we have drifted and drowned in the three miserable realms, enduring the suffering of birth and death, being covered in fur and bearing horns, and undergoing all manner of useless sufferings such as the iron beds and copper pillars.
If so, how could a Bodhisattva today—who performs the myriad practices for the sake of saving sentient beings—not be able to do it?
One must have the threefold faith in Amitābha Buddha’s immeasurable wisdom and immeasurable supernormal powers.

As well as the accomplishment of immeasurable powers of aspiration and other such matters, I too shall attain them. The Tathāgata’s essential nature and skillful means possess such inconceivable qualities;

because my own self-nature and that of the Tathāgata are identical in their purity, Amitābha Buddha neither departs nor arrives, and I likewise neither depart nor arrive. Between the Western Land and this realm—there is no separation.
Separated by the tip of a hair, yet one sees them as soon as one wishes to see. Why is this? Because all Buddhas take the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) as their body and land.
From the stage of the five faiths, Amitābha Buddha’s cultivation spans kalpas until the realization of the fruit, without shifting for even a single kṣaṇa.
I, too, shall not shift for even a single kṣaṇa; my station shall be equal to that of all Buddhas. Why is this?
Because "time" is comprised within karma, and within the ocean of the *dharmadhātu*, karma cannot be found. To have such faith and understanding is the initial mind entering the Way.

It is the practice of the pure lands of all Buddhas. Second, regarding the practitioners of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*: the Three Contemplations (*sanguan*) of the Tiantai school demonstrate the "fish-trap" of the single mind.
The "Hoof" (Tí) [section] summarizes the essential points of all dharmas. Each of the sixteen contemplations of the West possesses these three meanings. The *Miaozongchao* states:
"The three virtues within the nature are, in essence, the three bodies of the Buddhas; these very three virtues and three bodies are my own one mind and three contemplations.
If it were otherwise, then the Buddha would exist apart from the contemplation, and the object would not be identical to the mind; how then could it be called 'Perfect'?"

The school’s contemplation of absolute transcendence may likewise take Amitābha’s three bodies as the *dharmakāya*, my own three contemplations as *prajñā*, and the vision of the Buddha through the perfection of contemplation as liberation. Each one encompasses all three, like the new form of the letter *i*.

Since this is the case for contemplating the Buddha, the principle of contemplating all environments and inhabitants (*niśraya* and *adhiṣṭhāna*) is not a different path. As explained extensively in the commentaries and sub-commentaries, I cannot describe it in full here; you should understand this.

This means that one knows that a single recitation of the Buddha’s name fully embodies the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*). To realize that the mind which recites is neither the physical heart-mass nor a reflected image is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).

To realize that the Buddha who is recited—whether as the primary figure or the retinue—is each a perfect fusion of principal and attendants is the contemplation of form (*ākāra-vipaśyanā*). This realization is itself the contemplation of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad-vipaśyanā*). Thus, a single recitation of the Buddha’s name is endowed with these three contemplations.

To exhaustively penetrate vertically and pervasively in all directions is the provisional contemplation (*parikalpita*). To realize that subject and object are beyond dependence, such that both are simultaneously negated and both are simultaneously illumined, is the middle contemplation (*madhyama*).

Furthermore, the contemplating subject is itself the three contemplations within one mind; the contemplated object is itself the three truths within one realm. Since subject and object are non-dual, truth and contemplation are non-dual.
The three truths are the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); the three contemplations are wisdom (*prajñā*). The non-duality of truth and contemplation is the characteristic of Buddha-remembrance.
It is so. This is liberation. To raise one is to encompass the three, like the letter "I" in its new form.

Thus, a single invocation of the Buddha's name can purify the four lands, just as picking up a single atom transforms the great earth into gold. This is called the inconceivable contemplation gate of the perfect fusion of the Dharma-realm.
Regarding the practitioner of the three and six perfections, the *Śraddhotpāda Śāstra* states: "When the Bodhisattva’s profound understanding manifests before them..."

One cultivates the characteristic of detachment. Because one knows that the essence of the dharma-nature is detached from stinginess and greed, one practices the *dāna-pāramitā* in accordance with it.
Because the dharma-nature is unstained and free from the faults of the five desires, one practices the *śīla-pāramitā* in accordance with it. The dharma-nature is without suffering.
Because it is free from anger and affliction, one practices in accordance with the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).

Because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is devoid of the characteristics of body and mind, and because it is free from indolence, one practices in accordance with the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*). Because the nature of phenomena is eternally concentrated and its essence is without distraction, one practices in accordance with the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*).
Because the essence of the nature of phenomena is luminous and free from ignorance (*avidyā*), one practices in accordance with the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*).

If one cultivates the Pure Land through the *pāramitās*, one does not transcend a single practice. Thus, regarding these six meanings: in every thought-moment, one departs from [worldly] conduct by practicing giving;

in every thought-moment, one purifies conduct by practicing precepts; in every thought-moment, one practices tranquility by practicing patience; in every thought-moment, one continues the practice by practicing diligence; in every thought-moment, one practices the singular [path] by practicing meditative concentration;
and in every thought-moment, one practices the Buddha-way by practicing wisdom. One should know that departing, purifying, tranquilizing, continuing, and the singular are [all unified].
All phenomena necessarily arise in accordance with conditions, yet they all emerge from the addition of mindfulness of the Buddha (*nien-fo*). Thus, practice and assistance are non-dual;

phenomenon and principle are non-dual. For this reason, the single practice of mindfulness of the Buddha can encompass all practices, because mindfulness of the Buddha is the Dharma-gate of the one mind, and there are no practices apart from the mind.
If one were to abandon these practices, it would be equivalent to abandoning the mind itself.

Fourth is the practitioner of compassionate vows. The ocean of the nature of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is inexhaustible; their offerings are inexhaustible, their precepts and generosity are inexhaustible, and their benefit to others is inexhaustible.

Therefore, in the *Fivefold Contemplation of the Pure Land* by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, the four practices of prostration, praise, making vows, and contemplation are established as the gates of merit for entry, dedicated toward all afflictions and sentient beings.

Birth. To uproot the sufferings of the world and to accomplish the gateway of transcendent merit, the Bodhisattva cultivates the five gateways of mindfulness (*pañca-smṛtyupasthāna*) and swiftly attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Objection: The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* states that one should contemplate sentient beings as being like what is seen in a dream; once awakened, they are non-existent.
If one then makes vows to benefit sentient beings, is this not like seeing empty flowers with one's eyes? Answer: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* quotes the Buddha as saying: "There are no..."

"Buddha" means to destroy attachment to the notion of a Buddha; it does not mean to grasp at the mark of a non-Buddha. One should know that "no sentient beings" means to destroy the notion of sentient beings;
it does not mean to grasp at the mark of no sentient beings. Therefore, Vimalakīrti said that when a bodhisattva has performed such contemplation, he says of himself:
"I shall preach the Dharma of 'no sentient beings' for the sake of sentient beings. This is called true compassion. Thus, one knows that [this is] Bodhi...

The Bodhisattva saves sentient beings through various means; this is because he has profoundly realized the meaning of the non-existence of sentient beings. If one perceives the existence of sentient beings, one perceives the existence of a self;
with such inferior compassion, how could one perform these two kinds of beneficial practices? The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
The retribution for meritorious deeds is profoundly deep. There is no one like me who understands the measure of gratitude.
It was because my original desire was never satiated that I attained Buddhahood; now, although there are no further merits to be gained, my desire does not cease.
You should know that the ocean of practice is boundless, and its depths cannot be fathomed by a mere bamboo pole or a foot-measure. When a foolish child sees others...
Pointing to a pole in front of the gate, he said: "It is halfway to heaven. He then calculated and said: "From the earth to the heavens, it is only about two poles' distance.

The conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) of the Buddha-dharma is likewise so. Fifth, regarding "acting in accordance with the Dharma": the ocean of the Dharma-realm is immeasurable and boundless, and the ocean of practices is likewise immeasurable and boundless.
Therefore, all the practices of a Bodhisattva accord with their own nature; they do not exist [as independent entities].
It is not non-existent; it is neither acting nor non-acting. It accords with the self-nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). It is not attained by the initial mind, nor is it attained by the final mind.
Now, its characteristics shall be briefly set forth. A single bodhisattva brings all sentient beings to ultimate *nirvāṇa* without remainder, yet the realm of beings does not diminish.
It is like puppets upon a stage: their sorrow and laughter are vividly apparent, yet they are nothing but clay and earth, empty and devoid of substance.
There are. Second, there are bodhisattvas who practice the five acts of immediate retribution yet remain free from affliction or anger;

they enter hell without the stain of sin, and enter the realm of animals without the faults of ignorance, pride, and so forth—just as a woman’s *bhūta* (soul) departs and returns to give birth to a child, while her body remains constantly before her mother.
Third, there are bodhisattvas who enter meditative absorption with their own bodies and arise with the bodies of others; they enter absorption with a single body and arise with many bodies.

Sentient beings enter meditative absorption while insentient bodies arise, like a fierce tiger reviving a corpse that kneels, prostrates, and dances according solely to the tiger’s will, yet the corpse remains devoid of consciousness.
These four Bodhisattvas turn the Great Wheel of Dharma within the bodies of small sentient beings, kindle the great torch of Dharma, and thunder the great drum of Dharma;
the palaces of Māra are destroyed, the earth trembles, and immeasurable, boundless beings are delivered.
Sentient beings do not perceive or know this. It is like when a celestial musician enters the nostrils of a young girl;

yet the girl does not perceive or know it. If the five bodhisattvas wish to remain in the world for a long time, they can, in the space of a single thought-moment, expand it to immeasurable, countless hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas.
If they wish to remain in the world for a short time, they can [contract] the immeasurable...
Hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas are condensed into the duration of a single thought-moment, like a child watching horses gallop within a lamp-light;
from beginning to end, their quantity cannot be grasped.

If one realizes such inconceivable practice, the pure lands of all Buddhas of the three periods of time are entirely subsumed within a single thought-moment. This is called the Bodhisattva’s adornment of the pure land.
This practice can be seen by illuminating it with non-conceptual wisdom; it cannot be fathomed by the measures of the ordinary mind.
Why? Because its self-nature transcends all measures.

Recorded by Yuan Zhongdao on the fifteenth night of the tenth month in the Jia-yin year of the Wanli era. Having finished my daily recitations, I sat cross-legged in meditation. Suddenly, I fell into a deep trance as if attaining samādhi.
In an instant, my soul emerged from the house; the moon was at its brightest. Unconsciously, I rose light as a feather, moving as swiftly as a bird through the clouds. Within the clouds, two...
The boy called out to me urgently, "Follow me! and we proceeded westward. Looking down at the cities and villages, they appeared like beehives or anthills.
Suddenly, the two boys descended to the ground and said, "Stop. I followed them down and saw that the walls and roads were as straight as cords and as level as the palm of a hand.
Looking at the ground, it was not sand or stone; it was radiant, smooth, and glossy. Along the path there were channels made of patterned stone.
The embankments were some ten *zhang* wide; within the channels grew lotuses of five colors, their fragrance being extraordinary.
Above the channels, tree branches and leaves shimmered brightly, while beautiful birds sang in harmony. Interspersed were golden bridges spanning the channels with railings intricately interlaced.
Within the trees stood pavilions, magnificent beyond compare. The people within these pavilions were pure, elegant, and lovely, appearing as if they were immortals; they all looked at me and smiled.
The youth moved swiftly; I could not catch up with him. I called out loudly, "Please wait a moment at the Golden Bridge.
The youth did as he was told, and only then did I reach him. We leaned against the jeweled balustrade of the bridge for a short rest.
I bowed and asked, "Who are you? Where is this place? I beg you to tell me. He replied, "I am an attendant to Master Linghe. The Master has something [to discuss] with you..."
We met and spoke. I asked, "Who is this master? He replied, "He is your elder brother, Master Zhonglang.

"Then go quickly and speak of our meeting yourself," he said. We then took another path to a certain place where there were ten or so trees; their leaves were like emerald feathers and their flowers had golden petals.
Beneath the trees, the water in the pond gurgled, and above the pond stood white jade doors. One lad entered first, while another lad led us past.
The pavilions were more than twenty stories high, their golden hue shimmering brilliantly. Divine flowers and exotic grasses brushed against the eaves and pillars.

Arriving at the foot of one pavilion, a person came down to welcome him; his spirit resembled that of the Minister of the Interior, yet his countenance was like jade, and his robes were like clouds and mists.
Seeing him, he said with joy, "My younger brother has arrived! He took him by the hand and led him up the stairs to pay his respects. Four or five celestial beings then came forward to join them.

As they sat, the General of the Household said: "This is a frontier land of the West. Those whose faith and understanding are not yet perfected and whose jewel of the precepts is incomplete are mostly reborn here;

it is also called the Land of Indolence. Above, there are towers and terraces of transformation Buddhas. In front is a great pond, about a hundred *yojanas* in extent, within which are exquisite lotuses.

Sentient beings entrust their bodies to them, and when they are full, they disperse to dwell within the towers and terraces, where they associate with those of pure karma who share a karmic affinity."

Friends gathered together; because there were no seductive sounds or beautiful forms, their resolute understanding was easily perfected, and before long they advanced to become inhabitants of the Pure Land.
I privately wondered, "Is this still considered a borderland? I asked my brother, "Where were you born?

The Middle-Rank Officer replied, "Although my pure vows were deep, the taints of emotion had not yet been removed. I was first born here for a short time, but now I dwell in the Pure Realm. Thus it ended.

Your vehicle is swift, yet your precepts are lax; you merely dwell upon the earth and cannot ascend with the Great Beings (Mahāsattvas) to the precious pavilions in the void. You still require further cultivation.

Fortunately, because the wisdom of your past lives was sharp and keen, and because you once composed a treatise on the Western Land praising the Tathāgata’s inconceivable power to deliver sentient beings, you have attained mastery over flight and travel through various buddha-fields. Thus do the Buddhas speak.
The Dharma—all may go to hear it. This is truly supreme. I ascended slowly with La Yu; in an instant, we had traveled thousands of miles.
Upon reaching a certain place, I followed the Middle Rong down. There was neither sun nor moon, neither day nor night.

Its radiance was unobstructed, and its ground was made entirely of lapis lazuli. Inside and out, it was transparent and clear, with golden cords interspersed and interwoven, demarcated by the seven [precious substances].
The distribution of jewels was clearly demarcated. The trees were all made of sandalwood and auspicious; they stood in orderly rows, facing one another in tens of millions of layers.

From every single leaf emerged various wondrous flowers, displaying the colors of diverse jewels. Below them lay jeweled ponds, where waves rose up, producing immeasurable, spontaneous, and sublime sounds.
The sand at their bottom was pure diamond. Within the ponds were clusters of precious lotus petals.

The colored light shines upon the pond, where a series of perilous towers wind around it. Balconies extend out from the sides, their beams and eaves supporting one another, while windows and doors reflect each other’s light.
The steps, courtyards, balconies, and railings are all perfectly complete; there, infinite musical instruments resound, playing the sounds of all dharmas.
What is recorded in the Larger and Smaller Amitābha Sūtras lacks not even a hair’s breadth of discrepancy. Looking up and gazing at them, the pavilions in the sky are all like clouds and mist.
Zhonglang said: "What you see are the manifestations of the light of sentient beings practicing the path in the Pure Land."

Beyond this is the dwelling place of the Mahāsattvas of the Dharma-body; it is exceedingly exquisite, surpassing this by a thousandfold and ten-thousandfold, and their supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) likewise exceed this by a hundredfold and a thousandfold. By the power of my wisdom, I travel among them, yet I am unable to dwell there.
Beyond this is the abode of those in the Ten Stages and the Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*); even I cannot know it. Beyond this is the abode of the Sublime Enlightenment (*pratyakṣabodhi*).
"Only Buddhas and Buddhas can know this. Having finished speaking, they proceeded to another place. There were no walls or fences, yet there were railings and courtyards of extraordinary brilliance.
It was unclear what substance formed them; even gold and white jade appeared as if they were the color of earth.
They sat together beneath a pavilion and conversed for a short while. The General of the Household said, "I never imagined that such joy could reach such an extreme."

If I had strictly observed the precepts during my lifetime, it would have been even more than this. Generally speaking, when both the Mahayana vehicle (*yāna*) and the precepts (*śīla*) are urgent, one’s birth-status is highest.

Next, when the precepts are urgent and the vehicle is stable, one’s birth is most secure. If one possesses the vehicle but lacks the precepts, one is mostly dragged away by the power of karma and flows into the ranks of the eight classes of ghosts and spirits;
I have personally seen such individuals myself. My brother’s affinity for Prajñā is quite profound.
The power of their precepts and concentration is extremely slight. Indeed, to realize the principle without being able to give rise to precepts and concentration is also "mad wisdom";

it leads back to the five turbidities. While you are still strong and healthy, truly realize and truly practice; concurrently maintain pure vows, diligently apply skillful means, and have compassion for all beings.

Before long, you will naturally attain a noble awakening. If you enter another path, it will be terrifying and fearsome, as if one were unable to maintain the precepts—there is a dragon [that lurks there].

The method for observing the six fast days (ṣaḍ-upavāsa) established by Śrīghana still exists; follow it and practice it. The precept against killing is especially urgent. I address my fellow students:
if you have not yet set aside the carving knife and ceased the mouth’s craving for flavors, you will never be able to attain purity and peace.

Though one may preach the Dharma like clouds and rain, what benefit is there to such words? You and I were brothers in the world during the Kalpa of the Empty King, even as far back as the sixth [kalpa].

"In the Way, there is nothing that is not thus. I am fortunate to have attained a wholesome ground, yet I feared you might fall away; therefore, through skillful means and spiritual power, I have brought you here.

Since the pure and the defiled are separated, you may not remain for long. He then asked Boxiu about the places where his various relatives were reborn, saying, "The places of their rebirth are all excellent;
you shall know this for yourself later. Suddenly, he ascended into the air and departed. I followed him as he walked upon the surface of the pond.

He fell [into a swoon]. With a start, he awoke; sweat poured from his entire body. At that time, a dying lamp remained in its stand, and the bright moon shone through the window; it was already the fourth watch.
He replied to the scholar Zhuofazhi, "There is no difference between this and Chan."
Question: In the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka*, those of the two vehicles are like the blind and the deaf; yet, it also inclusively gathers the śrāvakas, for it encompasses immeasurable vehicles.

Although this sutra states that the seeds of the two vehicles do not arise, the dharma-factors (*dharmapada*) proclaimed therein are mutually accessible to both the Great and Small Vehicles, and are no different from the "Four Noble Truths" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka*. Therefore, there are those who are born into that sutra.

Regarding those who realize the small fruit only after an eon (*kalpa*): as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Amitābha also delivers sentient beings by means of the three vehicles (*triyāna*).
Since he himself should correspond to the Tripiṭaka, how can you say that the five teachings do not encompass the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) when they collectively subsume them?
Furthermore, if [the teachings] already pervade the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, could they not also pervade the immeasurable vehicles (*anantayāna*) subsumed within the *Avataṃsaka*?

Since the lay practitioner already knows that the *Avataṃsaka* subsumes immeasurable vehicles, how could he not know that noble śrāvakas such as Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana—who closed their eyes and silenced their hearing—did so entirely through the Tathāgata’s supreme power of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*)?

This was done to guide a certain class of those with limited capacities to give rise to deep faith and believe in the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "The Buddha, by means of countless skillful means..."
He guides sentient beings because, in reality, they all belong to the single Buddha-vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*).

This sutra states that those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) who do not produce [the roots of goodness] are specifically intended to convert and guide those of the two vehicles who cling to emptiness and do not cultivate the Pure Land. The Commentary says: "How could this apply only to ordinary beings?"
It also delivers the noble ones of the two vehicles. If even those of the two vehicles are born [in the Pure Land], how much more so will Bodhisattvas not be born?

Amitābha delivers beings by means of the three vehicles; one should have no doubts regarding this. Since he transforms and guides by means of the three vehicles, he also encompasses immeasurable vehicles. The two sutras are mutually consistent;
it goes without saying that they serve as analogies for one another.

Question: Studying the Way through other gates is called "ascending out of the triple world," while mindfulness of the Buddha for rebirth in the Pure Land is called "transversely exiting the triple world.
By "other gates" is meant, specifically, the contemplative practices (*vipaśyanā-caryā*) within the teachings;

thus, Zen meditation is termed the "separate transmission," and the Pure Land is called the "direct path," both because they transcend contemplative practice. Now it is said that contemplation is itself mindfulness, and mindfulness is...
This is contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). One might simply equate it with a multi-storied tower, but would that not leave the practice of *nienfo* (Buddha-recollection) neglected and rendered dull?

Regarding the "horizontal" and "vertical" discourse, the *Chao* states: "It is like a worm inside a bamboo; if it moves vertically, it is difficult to pass through the nodes, but if it moves horizontally, it is liberated all at once.
This means that the Land of Bliss and the realm of suffering stand side by side; hence it is called "horizontal. However, this is merely a provisional explanation.
Regarding the discussion of the one mind: it pervades both horizontally and vertically. The *Amitābha Sūtra* states: "The light of that Buddha is immeasurable;
it illumines the lands of the ten directions without obstruction. The *Contemplation Sūtra* states: "This mind creates the Buddha; the mind is itself the Buddha.

Since the Pure Land is solely mind, and because the realms are said to be horizontal, how could the mind not be perfectly complete? Other gates do not merely refer to contemplative practice (*guanxing*); in reality...
Thus, it encompasses all dharma-gates. That which is called the "separate transmission" of Zen is not what is expounded by the five teachings;

that which is called the "direct path" of the Pure Land is not what is reached through the three contemplations. Now, it is taught that contemplation is itself mindfulness, and mindfulness is itself contemplation.
To raise a single thought is to possess the practice of contemplation; by transcending with a single thought, one immediately attains rebirth. This is not [merely] the practice of contemplation.

[The practice] is perfected, and thereafter one is reborn. Thus we know that mindfulness does not hinder the inclusion of contemplation; it is not the case that the practice of contemplation can dull or obstruct mindfulness of the Buddha.
Question: The *Mūla-sūtra* states: "If there are sentient beings who give rise to even a single thought of mindfulness toward Amitāyus Buddha, they will certainly be reborn [there]."
Regarding that country, the commentary specifies a fixed period of up to ten recitations, yet does not mention even a single recitation.

Furthermore, the nature of recitation arises and ceases in a single kṣaṇa, whereas the power of concentration in this sutra arises only after seven days; thus, those who have not attained meditative absorption (dhyāna-samādhi) would have no share in it.

If this single recitation were equivalent to a single invocation, then the phrase "attaining Buddhahood" [in the text] would be interpreted as "single-mindedly taking refuge. This is the fundamental [principle].
One need not be bound by ten recitations; if one simply forms a single thought of joyful longing, one will attain rebirth even without any meditative concentration.
Furthermore, this superior expedient means should surpass that of the *Smaller Sutra*.
Since the ten recitations and this fundamental [single recitation] are mutually interpenetrating, how can one distinguish between their superiority or inferiority?

Because a single recitation encompasses all recitations, a single recitation is not necessarily inferior; because the ten recitations are identical to a single recitation, the ten recitations are not necessarily superior.
Therefore, it is said that a single thought-moment does not obstruct ten thought-moments, and ten thought-moments do not obstruct a single thought-moment.

Furthermore, the limit of a single kṣaṇa does not obstruct seven days, and seven days do not obstruct the limit of a single kṣaṇa. As the Sūtra says: "In a single thought-moment, one universally contemplates immeasurable kalpas."

There is no going, no coming, and no abiding. Whether it is said to be a single thought-moment, ten thought-moments, seven days, or many kalpas, these are all the supreme skillful means of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, one need not deliberate over whether [the state] is fixed or unfixed, nor over what is pleasant or unpleasant;
simply recite the Buddha’s name with a single mind, and there is nothing that cannot be accomplished. It is like a single grain of elixir that transforms iron into gold.
There is no further need for hesitation or anxiety. Furthermore, why must one compare the difficulty or ease [of practice] to determine its superiority?
A question was raised regarding these seven days: if one were to set them aside during ordinary times and only contemplate them when facing death, one would already be subject to Tianru’s reproach.
Now that this is indeed an ordinary time, [should one practice] after these seven days, or until the end of this physical life, never again [neglecting it]?

Is it that even if one subsequently becomes distracted and confused, one will ultimately attain rebirth? Or is it that if one never again becomes distracted, it should not be designated as merely "seven days"?
If one becomes distracted once more, then one has already regressed; how then could one cause the Buddha to manifest before him?
The Sūtra states: "One day, or even up to seven days" refers to rebirth within a fixed period. This does not distinguish between the time of death and ordinary times;

rather, it means that upon hearing the Buddha’s name even once, one immediately arouses a fierce and sharp resolve. As for those who attain rebirth within seven days, this is not the case for everyone.

If one has not yet attained rebirth, one must maintain an uninterrupted continuity of mindfulness from moment to moment—how could rebirth be guaranteed in exactly seven days? Furthermore, if one ceases to recite the Buddha’s name, the two [conditions] for maintaining the practice will fail.

Regarding the characters: How are they to be interpreted? The commentary states: "To uphold" (*dhāraṇa*) means that upon hearing the name, one receives it with courage and decisiveness, such that it cannot be shaken or taken away.
"To maintain" (*dhāraṇī*) means that having received it, one guards it, remaining eternally constant and firm so as not to forget it.

Why, then, would one allow it to dissipate again after seven days due to distraction? A practitioner should maintain single-minded right mindfulness, making it even more intense and vigorous for the remainder of their life. As...
At the very moment one first gives rise to this thought, why worry that the Buddha will not respond with grace?

The *Commentary* clarifies that "one mind" in the sense of principle constitutes the accomplishment of the power of contemplation; thus, thorough investigation belongs entirely to the gate of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
Previously, it was stated that wondrous contemplation (*miao guan*) is difficult to achieve; therefore, the superiority of holding the name (*chiming*) was revealed.

Now, however, you again advocate for the method of contemplation, which would still mean that fixed contemplation (*ding guan*) is superior to holding the name. If you claim that "investigating" the word "Who?

constitutes thorough inquiry (*ti jiu*), then this entirely belongs to the Chan school (*zongmen*). Furthermore, when investigating a critical phrase (*huatou*), there should be no discursive thought; thus, you inevitably fail on both counts.
How is this meaning to be reconciled?

The previous statement that "wondrous contemplation is difficult to accomplish" was intended to manifest the superiority of holding the name. This is because the beings of this Sahā world have minds that are largely distracted;

therefore, holding the name to collect the mind is superior to the gate of contemplation. Now, however, it is further reconciled with the method of contemplation, as the objects of contemplation differ.

It is superior. It does not hinder the swiftness of holding the name (*nien-fo*), for holding the name is a direct and expedient path; nor does it hinder surpassing the methods of contemplation (*guan-fa*).

Since both meanings are established, how can you say that [the former] falls short? If one investigates through the School of the Gate of the Patriarchs (*Zongmen*), this is a method suited to specific capacities and need not necessarily be harmonized with the Pure Land school.

For instance, if one investigates "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?", this immediately belongs to the realm where the path of words is cut off; furthermore, it cannot be [limited by such categories].
The logical path serves as a support.
Question: Since the general purport of this entire commentary emphasizes the maintenance of principle (*li*), the method of maintenance it elucidates is the most critical point.

Now, since this involves the maintenance of the name (*nien-fo*), and furthermore specifies the contemplation of principle (*li-kuan*); and since it is already a contemplation of principle, yet further introduces the "head of the story" (*hua-t'ou*) of Chan.
The three dharmas of śamatha, vipaśyanā, and purity are intermingled; although their principles are perfectly harmonious, the practitioner’s mindfulness does not converge upon a single point.
What, then, shall be taken as the primary tenet? How, moreover, can this differ from the principle of entering through a single gate and practicing with uninterrupted dedication?

The *Shuchao* (Commentary and Sub-commentary) in one volume, although it entirely returns to the contemplation of principle (*li-guan*), as Yuan Tan said: "If one observes the essentials, then simply practice the holding of the name.
He further stated: "To utter its name is to simultaneously possess all virtues; to focus exclusively on holding it is to encompass all hundred practices without omission.

Thus, we know that the exclusive practice of holding the name does not hinder the illumination of the contemplation of principle. When the contemplation of principle is clear and penetrating, it is like...
Adding fat to a fire only increases its fierce intensity. Likewise, the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra subsumes immeasurable vehicles;

for those of superior faculties and sharp wisdom, every aspect is a path, yet this is not called a confusion of teachings. It is simply that the capacities of the practitioners correspond to one another—this too is the skillful means of our venerable teacher.

The Commentary asks: "The statement that reciting the Buddha’s name with a sincere mind (*zhìxīn*) even once extinguishes the heavy sins of birth and death from eighty billion kalpas refers to the 'principle single-mindedness' (*lǐ yīxīn*).

If it concerns 'phenomenal single-mindedness' (*shì yīxīn*), then many recitations are required to merely extinguish minor transgressions. It then further cites the *Sūtra of the Names of the Buddhas*, which states:
"Hearing the names of the Buddhas even once extinguishes the sins of birth and death from immeasurable kalpas," and explains that "hearing even once" means...
It does not depend on recollection; "immeasurable" does not refer merely to eighty billion kalpas.

That being so, why must one point specifically to the single-mindedness of principle? Within this context, there is a self-contradiction. Furthermore, this sutra also states that those who hear the sutra or hear the name all attain non-retrogression;
thus, even those who casually make vows or call upon the name with a distracted mind shall all be non-retrogressive.
[This is] erroneous.
If one attains single-mindedness (*ekacitta*), then one need not distinguish between principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*).

As for the commentaries stating that "stopping many thoughts extinguishes minor transgressions," this is said from the perspective of those who, amidst distraction, hope to attain single-mindedness. Regarding the teaching that "hearing the name extinguishes sin," sentient beings are likewise immersed in delusion.

Furthermore, it is not known how many attain ultimate realization and achieve rebirth in the Pure Land merely by hearing the name of the Buddha—just as those in hell do—let alone the extinction of their karmic offenses.
This depends entirely on the diligence or indolence of the sentient being’s own mental power.

Generally, when the teachings discuss principle versus phenomena, or concentration versus distraction, they are like the rules of military strategy: victory in battle depends ultimately upon the individual. One must certainly not...
Once the ritual procedures have been definitively established, one may then proceed to the formal discourse.
Question: Zao Bo stated that the Great Way of the One Vehicle of the *Avataṃsaka* is not within the realm of bodhisattvas who aspire for rebirth [in Sukhāvatī].

Why, then, does the "Elder Son" of the *Avataṃsaka* lead them back to Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*) by means of the ten vows? Furthermore, Master Daosheng spoke of the existence of *icchantikas*. [Why is this?]

Regarding the Buddha-nature, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is cited as the subsequent proof. Now, since the current practices and vows do not at all accord with those of Zao Bo (Zhiyan), where, then, shall the fundamental tenets of this treatise find their refuge?
Consequently, even though Yunqi merely extracts the passage concerning "guiding back" (*daogui*), he is likewise unable to refute the errors of Zao Bo.
One must realize that Zao Bo is not easily subject to light-hearted disparagement; if one now wishes to harmonize [the two], [one must proceed with care].
Regarding these two points, what are their explanations?

Zao Bo (Zhiyan) maintained that the *Avataṃsaka* is not within the realm of bodhisattvas who aspire for rebirth [in Sukhāvatī]; this was to manifest the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), and thus it did not preclude disparaging the former while exalting the latter.
That Samantabhadra leads beings back to the Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*) is precisely because he encompasses the infinite vehicles (*anantayāna*). Zao Bo acted thus to transform the great...
Because ordinary beings enter the Flower Treasury World (*Huazang*) instantaneously through the mind, and Samantabhadra is the bodhisattva within that Flower Treasury World.

To lead those who take the ten vows as their guide back to Sukhāvatī is for the sake of universally benefiting those of the three capacities; it is like entering one corner by observing the directions, whereby the ten directions manifest everywhere.
This is because a great resolve is difficult to arouse, whereas birth in Sukhāvatī is easy to achieve. Thus, the ultimate destination and the essential aim coincide in both cases.
Thus we know that Daozuo and Daobo were not at all mistaken; how could Yunqi possibly consider them wrong?
One asks: many sutras speak of practitioners of *nianfo* who see the Buddha before them, such as Master Huiyuan’s three visions of the Holy One and others.
As it is said, "The Buddha dwells upon the crown of the head of the one who recollects Him. The ancient masters taught people to seek their resolve and seek its verification.
This is the case during ordinary times. Now, this sutra speaks only of the Buddha’s appearance at the moment of death.

Could it be that the merit accumulated over seven days is not sufficient for a direct manifestation, and one only experiences it at the end of life? Or must one first see him appearing before oneself, and only then see him at the moment of death?
Many sutras state that practitioners see the Buddha in the present; there are also expressions concerning seeing the Buddha in the future. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:

"If one recollects the Buddha and mindfulness of the Buddha, one will certainly see the Buddha both in the present and in the future. These two characters, "certainly" (*bìdìng*), carry profound significance.
It is like sowing grain and obtaining grain; there is never a case where the labor is wasted. Master Huiyuan beheld the sacred image three times.
This is seeing the Buddha in the present. When masters of the Pure Land school experience the Buddha coming to welcome them at the moment of death, this is seeing the Buddha in the future.
Viewed in this light, one need only fear not reciting the Buddha’s name; one does not need to fear that the practitioner will fail to see the Buddha.

Whether for a lifetime or for seven days, as long as one maintains single-mindedness without distraction and exclusively upholds the Name, one awakens the Amitābha of one's own inherent nature. All...
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas all manifest as reflections within it.

[The questioner] asked the World-Honored One: "Among those who practice, if one takes the mind that grasps at objects (ālambana-citta) as its own nature, it is like boiling sand in the hope of producing a fine meal.
Is the mind that now recollects the Buddha also a mind that grasps at objects, or is it not?"
If one employs a mind that clings to objects (*ālambana-citta*), then all discernment, observation, and contemplation are the very root of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
If it is not a mind that clings to objects, how can one speak of the nature of mindfulness arising and ceasing? Cause and effect are distinct in their resonance.

If you claim that this mind of arising and ceasing is itself the mind of non-arising and non-ceasing, why is it like "cooking sand"? This is what the *Lotus Sūtra* refers to when it says: "If a person scatters..."
Even with a distracted mind, if one recites "Namo Buddha" once, it is said that the succession of a hundred thoughts will not cease.
When the mind arises in response to objects, is this not simply using this very mind of arising and ceasing?
The World-Honored One refuted worldly people’s identification of the攀緣心 (攀緣心; *pān-yuán-xīn*, the攀緣心 or "clinging-and-conditioning mind") as the self-nature (*svabhāva*);
he did not refute the use of the攀緣心 to enter into the self-nature. Have you not heard what the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* says: "Using illusion to cultivate illusion"?

Tiantai exclusively employs the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*). Ānanda said: "Making offerings to the Tathāgata is also by means of this mind; the perpetual regression of the roots of goodness is also by means of this mind. Based on this inference...
This mind is not evil; it can serve as the vanguard for entering the Way. If one discusses the true nature (*dharmatā*), what need is there for mindfulness?
If one discusses the Land of Bliss, nothing will arise without mindfulness. Mañjuśrī said, "The nature of mindfulness arises and perishes.
This was his selection of the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty. How could a person of pure karma and wisdom allow themselves to follow after Mañjuśrī’s heels? If Mañjuśrī were to practice...
Regarding the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi*, you should take my mindfulness of the Buddha as your excellent guide.

With a single recitation of the *Lotus Sūtra*, afflictions arise and yet the Buddha-way is accomplished; with the unceasing [practice] of Nanquan, delusive thoughts emerge and yet Nirvāṇa is manifested.
Furthermore, I shall wait for another time to explain each point in detail to you, Layman.
Regarding the "Chui-ding Nianfo" (Mindfulness of the Buddha by Following the Peak) method, Chan Master Yizhao of Sanfeng quoted the *Book of Changes*:
"When one stills the back, one does not perceive the self; walking in the courtyard, one does not see the person.

This refers to the point where one ceases further effort in the pursuit of great learning. How much less could it apply to seeking rebirth in the Western Paradise through the method of mindfulness of the Buddha?

This is a matter of great inquiry: how can one who has spent their entire life merely parroting through rote memorization—only to reach a state of stunned unconsciousness at the moment of death—still wish to employ the practice of mindful recitation of the Buddha's name as a means of self-grasping?
This is certainly not so; what is precious lies in applying effort during ordinary times. First, there must be a point where one rests.
Once there is a place to rest, the mind becomes settled and joyful, and one has no anxiety regarding birth or death. Within this, it is empty and void, without any substance.
Thus, there is a spontaneous and unexpected foreknowledge that the time has arrived; a spontaneous and unexpected freedom from pain and suffering;
a spontaneous and unexpected state of fainting; and a spontaneous and unexpected rebirth by transformation within a lotus flower.
One should know that the *Smaller Amitābha Sūtra* merely provides a seven-day grace period for those who have failed to achieve merit through diligent practice.
After the work is accomplished, all that remains is a state of vast, silent, and unconditioned practice (*anābhoga-caryā*).
Therefore, when such a person approaches the end of life, their mind will not become inverted, and they will immediately attain rebirth [in the Pure Land].

If, however, one has not reached the state of "one-pointedness of mind" during ordinary times, then at the final moment of terminal agony and fainting, one will inevitably become terrified and mentally inverted, ultimately following along with [the delusions of the dying process].
Karma departs. If one exerts effort at this very moment, would that not be like "stiffening the calves," resulting in a lack of freedom?

Now, because my seclusion in the mountains has reached its peak, I have composed two hundred verses on the Pure Land and set forth the method of "chasing and topping" the Buddha-name recitation (*zuǐdǐng niànfó*).
My intention is for everyone to prepare in advance for the place where one lays down their tools; it is not that I dare to chew over the leftovers of others.
This is a culinary delicacy; it is the linguistic study of the Pure Land.
I hope that those of like mind will strive with a single, fierce resolve to bring it to completion, so that they may spend their entire lives as joyful people. This is my wish.

Regarding the essential requirement for mindfulness of the Buddha—that the mind be single-minded and undistracted—it means to single-heartedly recite a single phrase of the Buddha’s name with all one's might, striving with ever-increasing intensity.
Once deluded consciousness is severed, thoughts of the past no longer arise; speculations regarding the future do not take hold;
and the mental consciousness does not grasp at present objects. When these three types of mind are cut off, it is called the severance of the prior and posterior limits. This is the cause.
Pursuing to the ultimate and contemplating to the extreme, at the mere hearing or seeing of anything, whenever encountering conditions or stimuli, the pathways of the mind are immediately severed.
One directly attains the state where empty space is pulverized and the great earth sinks away; subject and object vanish together, and not a single dharma is established.

Before one’s eyes, all things appear like the myriad phenomena reflected in a great round mirror—utterly devoid of even a single point that can be pointed to, conceptualized, or distinguished. Body and mind are completely swept away.

When the clouds first begin to drift away, this very state is called "single-mindedness without distraction. This is because, upon reaching this point, there is no longer a mind that can be distracted.
If one does not reach this realm, although there may be temporary purity, it is merely a place of brief rest.
Such purity exists when one is still and is lost when one is disturbed; if it is lost even during moments of disturbance, how much more so at the ultimate moment of death?
At the time of extreme agony and suffering, one cannot even endure the pain; how much less so at the moment of fainting?
It can be seen that the minor states of stillness experienced throughout one's life are merely matters pertaining to the periphery of the mind, intellect, and consciousness.

When one reaches the point of fainting, the clever mastery of the mental consciousness is of no use whatsoever. Lately, there has been a generation of people who are skilled at preaching about the Western Paradise and diligent in their ritual recitations.
All have once practiced the work of transcending delusion and fainting; yet when death arrives, many fail to maintain their guard and find themselves flustered and bewildered.
We must not remain ignorant of this failing. If one wishes to be liberated from this failing:

Setting aside those of great heroic resolve, the "single-mindedness without distraction" mentioned in the Buddha’s sutras is precisely the ultimate method of practice personally pointed out by our Buddha.
It consists of nothing more than upholding the four characters of the Buddha’s name: holding one phrase upon another, following one sound with the next.
One must exert oneself like a fierce general grasping a sword to seize a thief, pressing straight ahead without the slightest rest.
If one proceeds with such urgency, one will surely be able to shoot the horse and capture the king.
Such practice is not something that can be accomplished through leisurely effort over many years or months; nor is it something that only reaches its peak of intensity upon reaching old age.
Simply practice this for one day while you are healthy; once you have severed the mind-consciousness and attained the realm of the preceding light, you may then let go and rest.
Even when you reach the point of fainting—amidst extreme pain and suffering—it will be exactly as it was at the beginning when the past and future limits were severed.
Returning to the root and adhering to the essence, it is like water returning to water, or space merging with space; how could you not be free? Yourself.

Know that the effort does not depend on the merit of the Buddha’s name, but rather lies solely in applying oneself with all one's might to the four characters through "chasing and crowning" (zhuiding).
I exhort my fellow practitioners and good friends: try reciting according to this method for one day and observe.
If it is not accomplished in one day, rest for a day and recite again; or recite for two consecutive days, then pause and recite again; or recite for three consecutive days.
From four days up to seven days, or for one day or seven days within a single month—our Buddha has generously set these timeframes.

If the practice of mindfulness is not diligent and the seven-day period is not completed, one should调养 (nourish and regulate) the spirit for another seven days, making it a firm resolve to attain a state of single-mindedness without distraction. If this is not achieved, one must certainly not stop.
One can reach the Pure Land in a single lifetime; one need only plant the wondrous causes for the lotus flower to await the fulfillment of success in future lives.
To maintain "single-mindedness without distraction" is the fundamental rule from beginning to end. Those who are of the same flesh and bone as the lotus—each of you must exert yourselves!
In practicing the method of *zhuiting nianfo* (reciting the Buddha’s name while following the breath), both monastics and laypeople, as well as men and women, may all courageously engage in it.
However, men and women must occupy separate altars; they must not intermingle. On the eve of entering the retreat period, husband and wife shall sleep on separate small beds in a clean setting.
At the fifth watch, having bathed and washed, they enter the altar, letting go of mental consciousness, closing off external conditions, and shutting their doors to sever all worldly affairs.
After performing three prostrations of worship, there is no need for further elaborate rites. One should proceed directly before the Buddha to receive the precepts.

For those who have already received them, their *karmavācanā* (ritual procedure) is thereby purified. From among the assembly, one should select a person of wisdom to serve as the leader and manage the multitude.
They should hold up the four characters "A-mi-tuo-fo" (Amitābha Buddha) and recite them with focused mindfulness, one after another, without interruption.

One may raise the voice, but not to the point of injuring the vital energy (*prāṇa*). One must not suppress the breath, which would stir the fire of passion. One must not remain silent while straining, which injures the blood.
One must not be overly relaxed, which nourishes the consciousness (*vijñāna*). One must not be too still, which leads to dullness. Sit for one *kṣaṇa* (half-branch) of incense;
stand for one *kṣaṇa*; walk for one *kṣaṇa*; then sit again for one *kṣaṇa*. Begin again from the start, maintaining a uniform and uninterrupted rhythm. This applies to eating and drinking as well.
When entering the latrine, changing robes, or performing similar tasks, one should always maintain the state of the Buddha and refrain from speaking.

During morning gruel, light snacks, midday meals, evening gruel, and at all times regarding fermented vegetables or small side dishes, do not indulge in excessive spending or give rise to craving. Simply focus on the four characters of "Buddha.
