Like water released from a high mountain, it flows with surging power that cannot be blocked; it cannot be let go of, for it naturally flows through the mind-ground.

Focus the mind-consciousness; it has no place to settle. When the recitation reaches the second watch of the night, if you are utterly exhausted, it does not matter if each person goes to their own mat for a sleep.

Upon rising, continue the recitation as before. After one or two days, if the recitation is urgent and both body and mind are weary, it does not matter if you take a full day and night off to sleep deeply until you regain your composure.
Once you have regained your composure, you will feel a sense of refreshing clarity.
Eat plain rice and thin gruel with refined vegetables. However, you must not allow thoughts to arise or give rise to worldly toil.
If you feel your spirits flagging and thoughts begin to stir again, continue this practice for another day or two. Maintain the message of the practice;

let every thought correspond with it and let every mind remain unchanged. If you continue directly in this way for seven days, or if you feel weary or exhausted, it is permissible to end the period and wait.
He rose again. This was because the method of practicing the Way must not be disturbed by dullness (*styāna*) and agitation (*auddhatya*).
If, out of fear of dullness, one merely tries to dispel it, one is directly opposing dullness; the more one fights it, the more it increases.
It would be better to let the body sleep, for then dullness will naturally subside. If one is disturbed by agitation, and merely tries to dispel it, one is directly opposing agitation.
To engage in opposition is to increase the conflict; it is better to let the body sleep for a while. Once body and mind are at peace, agitation (*auddhatya*) will naturally subside.
To let go for a moment at the height of intensity is precisely where the mind and its objects come to rest. As soon as one awakens and returns, the spirit is doubly vigorous.
When one takes up the Great Name (*mahānāman*), it is ten times more brilliant. Before one’s eyes, all is pure like snow; every sound and every form is precisely the severing of the mind.
The sphere of consciousness is ineffably sublime; this is the Dharma-treasury that has personally realized its benefits. I pray that you will cultivate the land of the Western Paradise;
you must not fail to believe in it. However, one must not use this as an excuse for indulging in sleep.

You must know that when your practice reaches its ultimate point, if you do not allow yourself to rest, the *ābhāsvara-māra* (shadows of the aggregates) will arise, or you will suffer from illness—all of which results from excessive attachment and a failure to understand how to harmonize [the mind].
Regarding the fault of grasping: those who take responsibility for this matter must reflect deeply upon it.

The verses on the Pure Land do not contradict Chan, the Vinaya, or the masters of the sutras; one should maintain them thus, moment after moment, directed toward the Western Paradise, until all hatred and attachment within the Dharma are completely cast off.
The objective realm naturally produces lotuses from the pool of the pure mind.

At evening one hears the village wailing; at night one hears singing. Worldly affairs are unreliable and full of transformations. When both singing and wailing are forgotten, the mind is naturally pure.
There is only this single phrase: the Ancient Amitābha.
A single note from the bamboo flute rests upon the ox’s shoulder; the grass turns from green to yellow as the year passes.
Having herded this inch of mind back to the Pure Land, the white ox has no nose and requires no leading.
Seated, one cuts off both the mindless and the mind-possessing; where in the West could one seek further? A single roll of thunder sends forth the night rain;
it falls sparsely, striking the seven-jeweled forest.
A single color-wave contains flowers of four colors; their interlacing lights form a net that encompasses the sands of the Ganges.
Layer upon layer, the ten-fold bodies of the Buddhas open and close, as they discourse with me upon the Supreme Vehicle.
The cricket’s cry is plaintive, yet the wild geese have not yet arrived; amidst white clouds and blue peaks, I linger through the night.
Having long since been free from worldly concerns due to my simple and unpretentious nature, I allow myself only to plant the pure land of the lotus.
The mountain stream has just dried up and firewood is cut off on the ridges; the morning cooking worries the mountain dweller to death.
Because of this, he comes to see the bliss of the Land of Bliss even more clearly, and his recitation of the single phrase "Amitābha" becomes even more sincere.

Worldly affairs are crowded and bustling, yet old age does not bring their end; with hair turning white and thinning, one still rushes about in pursuit. When dwelling in the shade, both body and shadow come to rest together;
the single phrase "Amitābha" is the ultimate realization.

The eastern neighbor recites repentances for transgressions; the northern neighbor chants the sutras. The Buddha-dharma draws people along and refuses to let them rest. Only my own true method of rest exists:
with one phrase of Amitābha, I close the wooden door.
The earnest longing for birth is not a mere eccentricity; it is simply that the addiction to the toil of worldly existence has not yet been removed.
When both the Eastern Land and the Western Paradise are free from such addictions, one realizes non-remainder nirvana within the stillness of the lotus.
Who burned this ancient sandalwood cauldron? Yellow clouds drift slowly within the hall. Clearly remember the events of that time;
the body remains amidst the lotus fragrance, which has not yet faded.
All things are unreal; how lamentable is this Dharma of the final age! One’s own birth and death are likewise deceived. Even Amitābha is still recited with a thieving mind;
one refuses to truly and sincerely make a single total surrender.

To recite the six characters for a lifetime is difficult to accomplish; drifting and wavering while holding the name makes one's effort feeble. Only when the preceding and succeeding thoughts are severed does the mind finally become one-pointed;
one must boldly devote seven days with fierce and single-minded diligence.

If one day you truly sever [delusion] from before and after, you will remain in accord with it for the rest of your life without further thought. At the moment of death, you need not wait for others to come to your aid;
a lotus flower will naturally welcome you beneath your feet.
Cutting off past and future, pure mindfulness continues; the six sense-faculties are gathered, and long practice brings about single-mindedness. With eyes wide open, the hours of dawn and dusk pass;
beyond the window are the streams and mountains, and upon the pillow is the sound of the world.
Verses for Binding the Altar and Reciting the Mantra of Rebirth.
Master Ouyi bows his head to Amitāyus, who uproots the fundamental karmic obstructions, to Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and to the ocean-like assembly of Bodhisattvas and Saṃgha.
I was deluded by the light of primordial wisdom and fell falsely into the suffering of saṃsāra, which has not paused for even a moment throughout vast eons;

without rescue and without a place of refuge, I have only with difficulty obtained this human body, yet still encountered the turmoil of the kalpa-turbidity; though I have attained the status of a member of the Saṅgha, I have not yet entered the stream of the Dharma.
I witness the Dharma-wheel being destroyed; though I wish to pull it back, my strength is insufficient. This is truly because since beginningless time, I have not planted superior roots of goodness.
Now, with a resolute mind, I seek birth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, so that by riding the ship of my original vow, I may extensively deliver all beings submerged in the cycle of suffering.
If I do not attain rebirth there, I shall be unable to fulfill my vows; therefore, I must certainly leave this Sahā world behind.
Just as a person drowning first seeks to reach the shore quickly, I shall then employ the power of skillful means to rescue all those swept away by the violent current.

With a heart of utmost sincerity, a profound mind, and a mind of dedication, I have burned three incense sticks before my arm and established a pure altar for one week, single-mindedly reciting the *Wangsheng Zhou* (Rebirth Mantra), except during times of eating and sleeping.
By the power of this merit, I pray for certain rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*).
If I were to retreat from my initial resolve and not head toward the Western Land, I would rather fall immediately into the hells to cause me to quickly give rise to repentance;

I vow never to crave the realms of devas and humans, nor the state of unconditioned nirvana. I look up with longing to the Great Awesome Power, the Strengths, the Fearlessnesses, and the Unshared Qualities.
The boundless virtues of the Triple Gem bestow their empowerment upon Zhixu and others: may they subdue [afflictions] so that we do not regress, and may they embrace us so that we may flourish.

*Text for the Dedication of Merit after Performing the Ritual Platform and Reciting the Buddha’s Name:* I prostrate to Amitābha, To the Dharma protected by all Buddhas, And to the sages and worthies of the Pure Land. I pray only that you will compassionately grant your protection and sustenance.
Since beginningless time, Zhi Xu has been deluded regarding the principle of eternal abiding and has lost the light of wisdom. Turning his back on his own nature, he has suffered in saṃsāra in vain;
grasping at the deluded mind, he has forever remained in opposition to the true realm. Although his roots of goodness have emerged, he has entered the True Teaching and left the household life.

My past habitual tendencies have been particularly dense; though I have perfumed myself with samādhi, it has not been realized. With a resolute heart, I directed my mind toward the Pure Land, vowing to escape the wheel of suffering.

Yet, as my karmic resonance was not singular, the response of the Sage remained unmanifest. Thus, years and months have slipped by in idleness, and my aspirations have been lost in confusion—a state that is both painful and lamentable, like being without an island or a shore.
Now, relying on the sincere instructions of Śākyamuni, I shall recite the Name for seven days to cast myself into the immeasurable light of compassion for the remainder of this life.

Seeking deliverance, I take refuge upon the pure altar and single-mindedly invoke the Great Name. Whether in a state of meditative concentration or distraction, whether with discernment or without it, by relying on the Buddha’s wheel of compassion, my merit shall not be in vain.
I pray that through these merits and all roots of goodness, I may together with all sentient beings dedicate them toward peace and happiness.
It is my hope that in this present life, all demonic obstacles will be eliminated, and at the moment of casting off this body, my right mindfulness will be certain for even a single kṣaṇa.
Born before the Tathāgata, one receives the prediction of enlightenment (*bodhi-vyākaraṇa*) and fulfills the wheel of original vows.

As for the Dharma-gate of mindfulness of the Buddha, there is nothing particularly marvelous about it; its essential point is simply the power of deep faith and practice. The Buddha said: "If a person..."
"Simply recollecting Amitābha Buddha is called the unsurpassed, profound, and wondrous dhyāna. Tiantai said: "The four kinds of samādhi are all equally named 'recollection of the Buddha' (nienfo);
the nienfo-samādhi is the king among all samādhis. Yunqi said: "A single phrase of 'Amitābha Buddha'..."
It encompasses the eight teachings and perfectly subsumes the five schools.

It is a pity that people today regard the practice of nianfo as a trivial matter, claiming it is merely the work of ignorant men and women; thus, their faith is not deep and their practice is not diligent.
Day after day they drift aimlessly, and no pure merit is achieved. Even if some should skillfully devise expedients, wishing to deeply clarify this samādhi, whenever...

To take the investigation of "Who? as the ultimate upward path is not to realize that the present momentary thought—the mind capable of thinking—is fundamentally free from fault and transcends all duality.
There is no need for deliberate effort to achieve this transcendence; it is simply the Buddha who is being contemplated in the very phrase before you.
Fundamentally, this transcends emotion and is beyond conceptualization; why labor to speak of the subtle or discuss the profound? It is simply valued that one attains faith and maintains stability.
Proceed directly with recitation—whether ten thousand times a day and night, or five thousand, or three thousand—taking it as a standard that there shall be no deficiency.
Vow that for the remainder of this life you will never change. If you do not attain rebirth [in the Pure Land], then the Buddhas of the three periods of time would be... [lied].
This constitutes deceptive speech. One will attain rebirth and never again regress; all manner of Dharma gates will manifest before one.
One must strictly avoid being like Zhang San today and Li Si tomorrow. When encountering those of the Teaching School (Jiaoxia), do not think of searching for chapters or picking out phrases;

when encountering those of the Zen School (Zongmen), do not think of investigating questions and answers; when encountering those who uphold the Vinaya, do not think of donning the robes or using the alms bowl. This...

Then, head after head remains unresolved and case after case remains unclear. How could one know that when the recitation of Amitābha Buddha becomes mature, the ultimate teachings and principles of the Tripitaka and the twelve divisions of the canon are all contained therein?
The pivotal mechanisms of the seventeen hundred koans are also contained therein.
The three thousand dignified demeanors and eighty thousand subtle practices, as well as the three clusters of pure precepts, are likewise contained therein.
To truly be able to practice Buddha-recitation and cast off the world of body and mind is the Great Giving.

To truly be able to practice Buddha-recitation and no longer give rise to greed, anger, or delusion is the Great Precept-keeping. To truly be able to practice Buddha-recitation and not calculate right or wrong, self or others, is the Great Forbearance.
To truly be able to practice Buddha-recitation without even the slightest interruption or admixture of other thoughts is the Great Diligence. To truly be able to practice Buddha-recitation...

No longer do you allow yourself to be distracted by wandering thoughts; this is great meditative concentration (*samādhi*). You are truly able to practice mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*), undeluded by other paths;
this is great wisdom (*prajñā*). Test yourself: if body and mind, as well as the world, have not yet been set down; if thoughts of greed, anger, and delusion still arise spontaneously;

if notions of right and wrong or self and others still linger in your heart; and if interruptions and intermingling of thoughts have not yet been eliminated—[then you have not yet attained these states].

Even when [the mind] is exhausted, delusive thoughts still pursue it without being eternally extinguished; if various extraneous paths can still distract the will, one is not yet practicing true mindfulness of the Buddha.
To reach the state of single-mindedness without distraction, there is no other method:
at the very beginning of practice, one must use a rosary to keep track clearly, establish a fixed schedule, and ensure it is never missed. After a long time, this will become thoroughly proficient.
Do not dwell on your own thoughts; then, whether you count [the breaths] or do not count them, it is acceptable.

If, from the very first moment, you insist on speaking of "fine words," insist on "not being attached to forms," or insist on "learning perfect interfusion and mastery," all of this stems from shallow faith and a lack of diligent practice.
Even if you can expound the twelve divisions of the teachings and deliver seventeen hundred turning phrases, they are all nothing but birth and death.
Regarding matters on the riverbank: at the time of death, these will certainly be of no use. Take care.

As for the method of reciting the Buddha’s name (*nien-fo*) shown by Shifa Yuan, it values nothing more than genuine faith. First, one must believe that I am a Buddha who has not yet attained full realization.

Amitābha is a Buddha who has already attained enlightenment; his essence is non-dual with our own. Next, one must believe that this Sahā world is indeed suffering and that the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang) is the place to which one may return.

One should then fervently cultivate joy in the latter and aversion toward the former. Next, one must believe that every single movement and action in the present moment can be dedicated toward the Western Pure Land.
If one does not dedicate them, even superior-grade wholesome deeds will not lead to rebirth there. If one knows how to dedicate them, even if an action is performed erroneously—
Regarding evil conduct: swiftly sever its continuity and give rise to earnest and profound repentance. By the power of such repentance, one can even attain rebirth there;
how much more so for those who maintain the precepts and cultivate merit through various superior karmas—how could these not suffice to adorn the Pure Land?

It is only because the power of faith is not deep that superior karma sinks into the realm of outflows (āsrava). Furthermore, to wish to abandon this and seek another alternative is a grievous error. Simply apply [yourself further]...
Truly believing that all one's practices need no further alteration,
he showed King Xin Kui the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and earnestly praised its skillful means (*upāya*). One must know that there are worldly skillful means, such as giving and loving-kindness.
The mundane skillful means include such things as filial piety, fraternal respect, loyalty, trustworthiness, and so forth.
The supramundane skillful means include such dharma-gates as suffering, emptiness, impermanence, non-self, impurity, mindfulness of breathing, dependent origination, seclusion, and contentment.
The supramundane, unsurpassed skillful means include the ten pāramitās, the four means of integration, the four analytical knowledges, the eighty-four thousand samādhis, dhāraṇīs, and so forth.

Furthermore, there is an inconceivable and supreme skillful means: to believe with all one's heart that within one’s own nature there truly exists the Tathāgata Amitābha who has realized the Buddha-way in the Western Quarter, and that within the mind alone there truly exists the adorned world of Sukhāvatī.

With a profound mind and great vows, one resolutely resolves to seek rebirth there. Not only are these supreme skillful means the requisite provisions, but they also encompass both the mundane and the supramundane.
Every skillful means is none other than a voucher for rebirth. Within this Dharma gate lies the technique of turning iron into gold;
without passing through the kalpas of the śrāvakas, one suddenly ascends to the stage of non-retrogression—this is called the "Dharma beyond all dependencies."

I show Guo Shanyou the great ocean of the Buddha-dharma: faith is that by which one enters; wisdom is that by which one crosses over. If one possesses faith but lacks wisdom, there is none who does not weep at the fork of the road.
The Buddha said that in the final age, strife will be firm and persistent; though billions upon billions of people study the Way...

It is rare for even a single person to realize the fruits of enlightenment; one can only rely on the practice of *nianfo* (mindfulness of the Buddha) to seek rebirth in the Pure Land, thereby transcending the wheel of suffering horizontally.

In the past, there was a patriarch who initially practiced only by reverently prostrating to the *Lotus Sūtra*. When he reached the character for "excrement" (*fen*), he suddenly attained realization of the *Lotus Samādhi*.
There was also a practitioner of the *Lotus Sūtra* who came to Master Shouchang to request instruction, only to be rebuked by him: "You crowd of heterodox views!"
"Born without knowing good from evil, the Lotus Sūtra itself is Zen. Where else could there be a Zen to be investigated?
The man accepted this teaching with devotion and departed; in the end, he attained enlightenment through his recitation of the Lotus Sūtra.

If one holds fast to the conviction that the practice of *nembutsu* and prostration is the true cause for attaining Buddhahood, and remains steadfastly unswayed by the currents of the times, this is itself the light of great wisdom, transcending and ascending to purity.
In the Pure Land, there will forever be no suffering of weeping at the crossroads.
In response to the tea talk by Zuoche regarding the Chan vehicle and the Pure Land:
both are sublime and wondrous teachings; yet as the capacities and natures of sentient beings differ, one cannot help but teach according to their individual dispositions.
The supreme point transcends both purity and dhyāna; it is simultaneously dhyāna and purity. To speak of "investigating" (chan-jou) is already a concession made for those of inferior capacity.
A true great man should naturally believe with deep conviction that this very mind creates the Buddha and this very mind is the Buddha.

If even a single thought is separated from the Buddha, it cannot be called the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (*nien-fo san-mei*). If every thought is uninterrupted from the Buddha, what need is there for labor?
One further asks, "Who? and thus investigates the character "who" (*shui*). This, along with methods such as gathering the mind or counting the breaths, is not the ultimate matter of the Pure Land.

The ultimate matter of the Pure Land is this: there is no Buddha outside of mindfulness that is the object of mindfulness, and there is no mindfulness outside of the Buddha that can be mindful of the Buddha.
At the very moment one applies oneself correctly, one does not fall into the four propositions or the hundred negations; one presses through the entire body.
Upon entering, one sees only the light from a single pore of Amitābha Buddha, and immediately sees the infinite Buddhas of the ten directions.
By being born in a single Buddha-land, the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, one is simultaneously born in the pure lands of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
This is the path that points upward. If one abandons the Amitābha manifest before one's eyes for a so-called "intrinsic-nature Amitābha," and abandons the pure land of the West...
To speak separately of "the Pure Land of Mind-Only" is a case of confused error. The Sūtra says: "The Three Sages and Ten Saints dwell in the realm of retribution;
only the Buddha alone dwells in the Pure Land. This is a hammer blow to the back of one's head. Samantabhadra’s Ten Great Vows lead one back to Ultimate Bliss;
who would dare categorize this as a provisional vehicle? To mind the Buddha and recite His name requires no expedient means; it is spontaneously attained.

The mind opens. Who would say that this is merely a matter of trivial detail? If one can deeply believe in this gate, establish vows based on that faith, and give rise to practice based on those vows, then in every thought-moment, immeasurable Tathāgatas will flow forth, sitting everywhere throughout the lands as numerous as motes of dust in the ten directions, turning the Great Dharma Wheel and illuminating both past and present;
this is not beyond one's capacity. How much more so will it shake the great trichiliocosm?
Enough. If you wish to understand the affairs of the patch-robed monks, there is no harm in borrowing a verse from Zhongfeng to convey this message. The verse says:
"I have never spoken of the Pure Land apart from Chan; You must know that there is no Chan outside the Pure Land.
Having set aside both of these public cases, The Five-Petaled Lotus blooms upon Mount Xionger."
Master Jieliu Chan said that Master Xijishe once told Layman Ding Gengye:
"If worldly people wish to cultivate the practice of purity, they must not say, 'I am busy now;
I will wait until I have leisure,' or 'I am poor now; I will wait until I am wealthy,' or 'I am young and strong now; I will wait until I am old. If..."
If one’s allotted lifespan is fixed for constant busyness, fixed for poverty, or fixed for premature death, there will be no opportunity to cultivate pure karma;
one will suddenly perish, and though regret may follow, it will be of no avail. How much better it would be to exert oneself in cultivation while the body is still strong and healthy!
How profound these words are! Yet nowadays, those who possess faith and joy are few; even among those who can deeply believe in the Pure Land, because—
Those who merely follow their needs and wait until their lives have slipped away by negligence are as numerous as they are. You, Layman, are of naturally pure and prudent character;

having seen this patch-robed monk for but a short time, you were immediately able to awaken to impermanence and observe the long fast while serving the Buddha. This is surely due to the presence of karmic conditions from past lives.

However, the layman’s family has no permanent estate; they obtain their grain by renting out their lodging each year. Since the family lacks a permanent estate, it is evident that they are insufficient for their needs.
Since he holds the position of lodging-attendant himself, it is evident that he is not at leisure. Since he is only fifty years of age, it is evident that he has not yet reached old age.
Yet, all of a sudden, he resigns his post as attendant and does not go, turning away his disciples while maintaining—
He maintained the full precepts of an upāsaka, locking his door for the entire year and devoting all his efforts to pure practice. As for his provisions and water, he never kept accounts;
could anyone but a courageous man be capable of such a thing? Moreover, he did so even within a cramped room of but a few cubits.

Half of it was used for providing offerings for the scriptures and images. Within this space, he avoided the clamor of the world to rest his spirit and applied himself with keen resolve to diligent cultivation.
It was as spacious and comfortable as a grand mansion, and he lived there in tranquil contentment. Yet, he was only concerned that he might not be able to remain in such a state for long.

Alas! When a person dwells in this world, how can anything be taken as permanent? I have often reflected on this: there is no leisure greater than not losing the opportune moment; there is no wealth greater than...
One should always be content with what one has. In terms of strength, nothing is stronger than diligent perseverance. Now, the Layman possesses all three of these qualities.
Thus, even if one were to compare him with the most idle, wealthy, and powerful individuals in the world, I know that they would possess only fame but lack true substance.
Being able to act in this way—what difficulty could there be in being born in the Pure Land? Furthermore, there is...
Regarding the single phrase "I wish to exhort you": it is like a ten-thousand-hu vessel that wishes to travel somewhere;
its mast is not unlofty, its rudder is not unsteady, its provisions are not incomplete, and its resolve to depart is not uncertain.
Riding the wind with sails unfurled, one possesses the momentum to travel a thousand *li* in an instant.
Yet, if a single mooring stake at the prow has not been pulled out and one remains tethered by a single cable, how could various efforts to push and pull provide any relief?

Nowadays, those engaged in the practice of purity may spend their entire day reciting the Buddha’s name, repenting their sins, and making vows; yet the Western Land remains distant, and rebirth there does not occur.
"Preservation" means that there are no other attachments; it is because the mooring ropes of emotion have not yet been pulled out and remain firmly fastened.

If one can regard the affectionate ties of this Sahā world as being like chewing wax—regardless of busyness or leisure, motion or stillness, suffering or joy, sorrow or delight—and rely solely upon the single phrase of the Buddha’s name, remaining as immovable as Mount Sumeru, then no external circumstances or conditions will be able to shake them. Or, at times, when one feels weary of oneself...

When the habit-energies of indolence and delusion manifest before you, rouse yourself with a single thought like a long sword leaning against the heavens, causing the demonic armies of affliction to flee with no place to hide;
it is also like a fierce fire in a red furnace, causing the emotional consciousnesses of beginningless time to melt away without remainder.
Although such a person currently dwells in the land of the five turbidities, they have already sat their entire body within the Land of Lotus Flowers. What more need be waited for?
"Amitābha extends his hand and Avalokiteśvara urges him to board the carriage; it is only then that one truly believes in rebirth there.
Someone said, "If this layman was so courageous and diligent, how could he still be entangled by affection? Is this not like administering medicine to one who is not ill? I replied, "Not so.
An ancient said, 'If attachment is not heavy, one will not be born in Saṃsāra. And it is also said, 'If the thought of the Way is..."

If one harbors thoughts of compassion, it will take a long time to attain Buddhahood. Even the five-attainment immortals (*pañcābhijña-ṛṣi*), who exerted themselves with diligence over many kalpas, still fell from their meritorious practice because they had not yet eliminated the outflows of desire (*kāma-āsrava*).
Thus we know that until one has ascended to the fruit of sainthood (*ārya-phala*), there are few who are not bound and entangled by it.
Layman, you have indeed lightened worldly thoughts and possess a courageous and sharp resolve for the Way; you view desire as you would avoid a pit of fire. Recollect—
The Buddha is like a compassionate mother who cherishes her child; one should maintain pure fasting and daily recitations with a vow never to waver.
Furthermore, what harm is there in a healthy person constantly taking wholesome medicine? Will it not lead to ease in daily life and even greater strength and vigor?

In short, while afflictions are inexhaustible and constitute the very root of birth and death, it is specifically craving that can drown the practitioner and obstruct the Dharma of rebirth in the Pure Land.
For this reason, the sutras of the former Buddhas reprimand [this attachment] in various places. If one merely thins out a portion of emotional affection, then a portion of pure karma will ripen;
thus, at the very brink of birth and death, one may hope to attain liberation. Layman, you must strive for this!
The West specifically points to the essential Dharma of the Buddhas and the Bodhisattva Jue-ming-miao-xing (Subtle and Wondrous Practice of Enlightenment).
It is subtle, secret, and inconceivable; because it is beyond thought and deliberation, no one can fully proclaim it.
The Muni, the Great Compassionate Father, who takes pity on all sentient beings, has spoken that which could not be spoken, guiding them through this life and into future worlds.
Furthermore, by means of diverse skillful expedients, he reveals the lands of peace and bliss, causing them to resolve to be reborn there and thereby cross directly over all evil realms.
Because Amitābha Buddha gathers all beings through his great vows, those who hear his name and are able to uphold it will certainly be born [in his land] without doubt.
If there is a person of great strength who focuses their mindfulness with a constant one-pointed mind and accomplishes the profound samādhi, they shall see the Buddha before them in the present.
Now, following the Buddha’s teaching, I shall open the gate of transformation and guidance. Considering your delusions and inversions, I firmly point out the path of correct cultivation.
This is no minor matter; you should conceive the thought that it is difficult to encounter. Though the journey to the West spans ten billion leagues, a single moment of faith is sufficient.
This single gate of the Pure Land shown here is the true heart-essence of all Buddhas and the direct path for humans and devas.
Although you now seek rebirth there, if your aspiration is not earnest, it will be like entering the ocean without obtaining a precious jewel; your toil will be in vain and of no benefit.
In the past, during the time of Emperor Ming of the Jin dynasty, I received the body of a poor man. Because of my poverty and suffering, I made this great vow, saying:
"I have received this bitter retribution due to my past karma.

If today I do not behold Amitābha Buddha, be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and accomplish all meritorious virtues, I shall lose my life rather than ever retreat from this resolve. Having thus sworn, I—

For seven days and seven nights, he focused his mind with single-minded devotion and mindfulness. Thereupon, his mind was opened and he beheld Amitābha Buddha, whose marks and signs and radiant light pervaded the worlds of the ten directions.
Before the Buddha, he personally received a prophecy of his future enlightenment.

Later, at the age of seventy-five, he sat in meditation and passed away, ultimately being reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Subsequently, due to the weight of his vow to deliver sentient beings, he returned to this world to manifest transformations according to the needs of various regions.

Sometimes appearing as bhikṣus, sometimes as lay devotees, sometimes as kings, sometimes as ministers, sometimes as women, or even as butchers—whether hidden or manifest, whether conforming to or opposing worldly ways—he preaches the Dharma in accordance with their needs to guide all classes of beings.
Now, he has once again appeared for you to clarify the distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox, and to expound upon the Pure Land. You should therefore focus your minds as one.

With single-mindedness, cultivate this gate with steadfastness; you shall certainly not be led astray. If your resolve is single and firm, you need not wait for a future life to be born [in the Pure Land];
you may behold the Buddha even in the present life. There is a four-line verse: "Speak but a single word less, recite a single name of the Buddha more.
Strike the thought-moment until it dies, and I grant that your Dharma-body lives."
Do you worry that your bodies are entangled in the worldly net, such that your thoughts cannot be pure?
I have a method for you: simply make a vow to distance yourselves from this world and seek deliverance.

By replacing the mind that rushes after fame and profit with a heart that resolutely turns toward the Land of Ultimate Bliss to behold Amitābha Buddha, you will be able to transform the very midst of worldly toil into a Pure Land.
Someone asked, "If one is unable to maintain single-mindedness in the practice of nianfo (reciting the Buddha's name), what expedient means should be employed?

The Bodhisattva replied, "You need only cease fixed conceptualization and recite slowly. You must ensure that the sound accords with the mind and the mind follows the sound; after a long period of such practice, you will naturally attain it."
All thoughts become clear and pure, and the mind and its objects are illuminated beyond duality; one thus realizes entry into the *nien-fo samādhi*.
However, in daily practice, one must recite the Buddha’s name many times—from a thousand to ten thousand—with the mind uninterrupted. Only then will one's faculties most easily reach maturity.
If one forces the mind to be single-pointed, it will ultimately never achieve such singleness.
Dingmao wished to abandon the recitation of mantras and practice mindfulness of the Buddha instead. He asked for instruction, and [the Master] showed him, saying:

"If you wish to abandon the recitation of mantras and practice mindfulness of the Buddha, it is most excellent to cultivate this with single-minded devotion. However, you do not yet understand the essential points of the Dharma;

you may only be called a person who observes the fasts and loves goodness, but you cannot be called a person who practices mindfulness of the Buddha. Why is this? To sail across the great ocean, one must necessarily..."
One who wishes to travel a thousand li in a great ship must first select a fine horse;

likewise, a person who recollects the Buddha must first possess great capability to sever all entanglements and tear open the net of dust. Directly and immediately, the recollection is the Buddha, and the Buddha is the mind.
Even to the point of transcending both "is" and "is not," one suddenly enters the Tathāgata’s Great Treasury of Radiance. Only in this way is it called "right mindfulness of the Buddha."
One is thus named a person who practices mindfulness of the Buddha. You should skillfully understand this meaning.
Disciples, you must know that the Buddhas of the ten directions are the minds of sentient beings, and the sentient beings of the ten directions are the minds of the Buddhas.
Therefore, when one recollects and mindfully contemplates the Buddhas, the Buddhas of the ten directions manifest within one’s own mind. Yet, they are not [separate from it].
The Buddha’s entry into your mind does not mean that your mind emerges from the Buddhas; rather, it is the wondrous, fundamental luminosity of awakening, which is inconceivable.
Where the movements of the mind cease, this is the eternally abiding true mind of all Buddhas. Where the movements of the mind exist, this is the birth and death of sentient beings.

This is the mind of karma; there is not even the space of a hair or a thread between [thoughts]. If you can apply yourself with such density that this mind leaves not the slightest gap, only then will you attain some degree of correspondence.
Do not practice carelessly for half a year or ten months and then claim, "I am able to cultivate the Way with diligent effort.
You do not realize that this is precisely what obstructs the Way. Be most careful of this. Furthermore, although your efforts—
Furthermore, if you have not yet reached the point where [the mind] is like a copper mountain or an iron wall—unshakable and immovable—it is still not yet "forged into a single piece.
Do not, upon seeing some slight sign or reflection, immediately stop your practice; this would be to abandon the path halfway through.
You will surely lose all prior effort, resulting in no benefit whatsoever. This is a great malady of those who study the Way, which one must recognize. One must know this.
The great ocean of the Buddha-dharma becomes ever more profound as one enters it; it cannot be exhausted by any minor knowledge or views.
One should practice throughout one's entire life, making the ultimate goal one's standard. By all means, do not regard it as something easy.
The samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha is accomplished by the great power of your own minds; it is not brought about by anything else.

Now, that your mindfulness of the Buddha during the day and night cannot be equal, and that distracted thoughts still intermittently interrupt the true state, is entirely due to your failure to apply your minds with sufficient power.
Gu Dingcheng requested instruction. He was shown this: "Good son, the mind is fundamentally without thought; thoughts arise following after perceptions.

These perceptions are illusory and false, causing one to transmigrate through birth and death. You should now know that this single phrase, 'Amitābha Buddha,' does not arise from perception, nor does it exist through thought.
It dwells neither within nor without, and it has no form or appearance. This is precisely the exhaustion of all deluded thoughts."
The Buddha-Tathāgata’s pure, subtle, and wondrous body of reality is neither one nor many, and cannot be differentiated.

One who contemplates in this manner will find that afflictions and worldly toil are neither severed nor bound; they cease to be anything other than the single mind, and one will surely attain that single mind.
Only then can it be called "upholding the Name," and only then can it be called "single-mindedness without distraction. When the merit of pure practice is perfected, one proceeds directly...
Advance to the superior grade. You should now make a great vow to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Thereafter, with utmost sincerity and deep earnestness, invoke the name of Amitābha Buddha, ensuring that the sound conditions the mind and the mind conditions the sound, so that sound and mind rely upon one another.
Just as a cat catches a mouse, do not let this lapse for a long time; then you will enter the samādhi of right mindfulness. If you wish to advance further, you should expand [the practice].
I consulted various masters and extensively inquired of those of lofty wisdom. Having personally realized the wondrous truth that "the mind itself is Buddha," I instructed Wuxiu, saying:
"In general, for one who cultivates the practice of purity, whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, or rising, resting, eating, or drinking, it is appropriate to face west.

In this way, the resonance between the spiritual capacity and its object will easily be achieved, and the faculties and their environment will easily reach maturity. Within the room, provide offerings to only one Buddha, one scripture, and one..."
There shall be only one brazier, one table, one bed, and one chair; no superfluous items are permitted.

The courtyard must also be swept clean so that walking meditation may proceed without hindrance. One must ensure that this mind is free from even a single strand of attachment, forgetting all myriad concerns.
It should be utterly empty and void, such that one is unaware of the body, unaware of the world, and does not even know whether what I am doing today is right or wrong.
Regarding the matter of spiritual practice: if you act in this way, you will draw closer to the Way day by day and become increasingly separated from the world.
You can thus advance toward pure karma. Indeed, at the time of your birth, you were born clean and left this world clean; not even a trace of a root or a knot remains within your thoughts.
When the great limit arrives, you will be composed and detached, without the petty attachments of children for body or home.
The manner of a son or grandson—is this not the conduct of a great man? This is precisely why I require you to practice with single-minded devotion, free from all lingering attachments;
it is for the sake of this one great point. As for the method of practicing the Pure Land, it does not go beyond the two characters "exclusive" and "diligent.
To be exclusive means to do nothing else; to be diligent means not to waste a single moment. You—
This morning, upon rising, I immediately recited one scroll of the *Amitābha Sūtra* and chanted the name of Amitābha Buddha one thousand times.
I then performed the dedication of merit before the Buddha, reciting the "Text on Single-minded Taking Refuge," as its words are concise yet comprehensive in meaning.
This constitutes my practice for this session. If, at the start, the body and mind are not yet settled, limit the practice to four sessions per day; once somewhat settled, gradually increase.
Increase this to six sessions, and further gradually increase it to twelve sessions, totaling twelve fascicles of scripture.

Recite the names of the Buddhas twelve thousand times, and during the time of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), perform one hundred prostrations to the Buddha. Alternatively, these may be divided into four sessions;
this constitutes the daily routine. As for other work, there is no need to calculate the number; whether done silently or aloud, simply collect the mind and maintain mindful recollection.

Furthermore, regarding the method of holding the Name: one must ensure that every syllable and every phrase is accompanied by both voice and mind, without allowing even a fraction of worldly thoughts to intermingle.
Through long-term cultivation until it reaches maturity, one will certainly attain birth in Sukhāvatī, sit upon a precious lotus flower, and ascend to the stage of non-retrogression.
If your remaining years have not yet ended, you may still serve as a guide for the fourfold assembly with what you have realized, thereby repaying the profound kindness of the Buddha.
If you follow every single word I have spoken, only then will you not fail the Bodhisattva Jue-ming, who showed you the right path and caused you to leave the household life.
This was no small cause or condition; do not harbor self-contempt, but be careful, be careful!
He further instructed him, saying: "The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* consists of twelve fascicles, and the names of the Buddhas number twelve thousand. Do not increase them;
do not decrease them. Simply follow my practice. However, the sutra must be recited with evenness and purity—neither slow nor hurried, neither too fast nor too slow."
Do not be slow. The Buddha requires that every sound and every thought be focused. Do not be harsh or agitated; do not be superficial or sluggish as you recite.
When it comes to the dedication of merit, do not merely chant the traditional text once; rather, you must give rise from within your own heart to a genuine vow for Great Bodhicitta.
With utmost sincerity and earnestness, universally pray that all sentient beings may be reborn together in Sukhāvatī, and that I—
When the mind is without attachment, equal to empty space, this is called dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). Furthermore, while sitting in stillness, one should reflect inwardly and investigate deeply:
the Buddha is none other than my own mind; this mind is the Buddha. There is no need to seek it externally. Abide as the mind is; there is neither subject nor object.

Contemplate thus with single-minded focus, without a second thought; this is called the cultivation of samādhi. Be careful not to lose your physical composure or allow your mind to die, lest you fall into the views of external māras.
Sit in this manner for a period of time, then arise and perform walking meditation (caṅkrama). Furthermore, there is a proper sequence for recitation.
If you are in a frantic hurry, rushing through it all at once in a single breath, thinking that you can thereby complete the day’s liturgical recitations, you are mistaken.
One will then harbor a mindset of mere expediency and superficiality; this is not genuine practice.

Generally speaking, if a student of the Way does not follow the clear instructions of their teacher, they will certainly labor in vain without benefit and will surely fail before long. Be careful, be careful!
In general, those who cultivate the Pure Land most dread "intermingling" (cluttering their practice). What is meant by intermingling?

It refers to reciting sutras, chanting mantras, organizing assemblies, and being fond of discussing trivial Zen, while also prattling about omens of good and ill fortune, calamities and blessings, or speaking of seeing ghosts and deities;
this, indeed, is intermingling. Once one intermingles, the mind will not [be focused].

Single-mindedness. If the mind is not single-minded, it will be difficult to see the Buddha and attain rebirth in the Pure Land; you would then have wasted this entire life in vain. From now on, do nothing else at all, but simply and firmly hold to one phrase:

"Amitābha Buddha. Set your goal on birth in Sukhāvatī. When the long duration of practice has brought success, you will finally avoid making a mistake. I grant you this verse; follow it and act accordingly. *A* (Verse) The mind is like a monkey, leaping about in the forest of phenomena; If you wish to tame it, you must first rely on the Buddha’s name. When the power of the name reaches its full measure, The monkey will naturally become still. Do not seek anything else; Simply recite the Buddha’s name with single-minded devotion. If you can maintain this for ten thousand days, You will surely attain birth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. *A* (Verse) If you wish to see the Buddha and attain rebirth, You must first cultivate single-mindedness. If the mind is not single-minded, It will be difficult to see the Buddha and attain rebirth. This would be to waste this entire life in vain. From now on, do nothing else at all;

Only firmly hold to one phrase: "Amitābha Buddha. Set your goal on birth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. When the long duration of practice has brought success, You will finally avoid making a mistake. I grant you this verse; Rely upon it and act accordingly. *A* (Verse)
The single phrase of Amitābha is the dhāraṇī that encompasses all phenomena. Sound and mind rely upon one another; as one recites, the focus remains ever-present.
Through inconceivable resonance and response, the lotus blooms in the pool of seven treasures.
Regarding the practice of *nianfo*, the *Zhang Guangwei Jing* states:
"Uphold the name with single-mindedness and without confusion. The two characters for "upholding" (*zhíchí*) pertain to the hands rather than the mouth.
If there were an object that could be grasped, it would not be a true grasping. The Confucians speak of being "earnestly devoted" (*quánquán fú*).
*Ying*: Zhu Xi’s commentary explains this as "the appearance of reverently upholding. This carries the meaning of grasping and maintaining.

What follows, "do not lose it," conveys the sense of not being disordered. The Confucian tradition also uses the term *gùtǐ*. Zhu Xi’s commentary explains this as "constantly keeping it before one's eyes.
This carries the meaning of forming a mental visualization, which is also synonymous with not being disordered. When reciting with the mouth and looking with the eyes, the ears naturally—
Listen. Sound flows from the tongue; the mouth partakes of the flavor of dhyāna; the nose smells wondrous fragrances; and the dust of the mind does not arise.
Reciting the Buddha’s name in this way, the six sense faculties return to oneness—how could there be distraction? Now, as I recite the Buddha’s name, I employ a skillful means:
I observe this mind as a pure jeweled vessel, and the Buddha’s name serves as its fine grain. With every word and every phrase, it is like pouring grain into the vessel.
The grains fell like a string of pearls. Though the grain was inexhaustible, the jar remained unfilled. Not a single grain was allowed to fall outside the jar.

He reflected that this jar was but a span in diameter, yet within it were contained three thousand great thousandfold world systems, as many buddha-fields as there are atoms in ten billion worlds, and thirty-six trillion, one hundred and eleven thousand, nine thousand five hundred Buddhas of identical name and title.
Amitābha Buddha dwells therein; I too shall join him in that same place to enjoy, rest, and find peace.
This alone shall be the ground upon which I establish my body and sustain my life. Nevertheless, I still have cause for concern: all the obscurations of ignorance are like rats and sparrows;
if my defenses slacken even slightly, they will consume my fine grain. Should I ever violate a *pārājika* offense, the Sangha—
The *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharma is like a precious vase falling to the ground and being shattered beyond repair; be careful!

Nowadays, there are many who practice the recitation of the Buddha's name (*nienfo*), yet they do not know that the character for "recitation" (*nian*) is derived from the heart-radical and is not merely a matter of the mouth.
If one uses only the mouth, the mind and the Buddha will not connect—what merit or practice can there be? The Master Tu Chui-shui said: "Those who recite the Buddha's name rely on..."
To restrain the mind with the mouth, reciting the Buddha’s name a thousand times while the mind wanders in myriad directions—what merit can there be in such a thing? Master Liu Yushou said:
"Among those who recite the Buddha's name several hundred times, it is often the case that upon reflection, their minds do not accord with the first phrase [of the verse]."
At this juncture, it is appropriate to bring this up for examination. Master Shiyu’s verse says: "When reciting the Buddha’s name, do not greedily seek to recite too much;
Recite even just one hundred times with an undistracted mind. If you miss even one of the ninety-nine recitations, The entire rosary is turned back and does not count."
In this manner, from one hundred to one thousand, and from one thousand to ten thousand, like beads strung together, they are impenetrable to arrows and unassailable by swords;
the armies of a million demons all flee in retreat. When mindfulness reaches the realization that both persons and phenomena are empty, one casts the prayer beads toward the Court of Non-arising.
Only through these three grades of mindfulness of the Buddha is one truly called a "True Buddha"; otherwise, it is merely a vain establishment of a daily regimen. Hurry! Hurry!
To understand this thoroughly: at the very moment of recitation, one does not even know where that which is called "Buddha" resides;
how much less so before the recitation has begun or after it has ended? In the past, my recitation of the Buddha’s name was merely a matter of reciting it as a whole.

Now I know deeply that every single character must roll forth from within the mind, and furthermore, every single character must penetrate back into the mind. Moreover, one should practice with this in mind.
He sat facing west with eyes closed in contemplation, silently visualizing that spirit and form were separating as he proceeded directly toward the west.

Gradually, groves of trees, waterfowl, golden cords marking the paths, and jeweled railings appeared before him; in succession, there were precious ponds with exquisite lotuses, fragrant altars, and multi-storied pavilions, all vividly manifest to his sight.
There stood the Buddha Amitābha, sixteen feet tall, with Avalokiteśvara attending to his left and Mahāsthāmaprāpta attending to his right.
He emits light from between his eyebrows and extends his hand to welcome us. I and all the superior virtuous ones are gathered within that light and follow it upward.
Prostrating at his feet with deep sincerity, I suddenly see a golden palm stroke my head and nectar drench my body. After a long while, the spirit gradually returns;
as if emerging from a state of deep concentration, one recalls the words of the ancients: "First send the mind back to the Land of Ultimate Bliss. This is the visualization.

It should be thus. I pray that you will instruct all those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha: one must understand that this is a matter of mental cultivation; do not merely recite with the mouth.
Then, naturally, there will be a path of entry.
Written after the *Jingtu yuoshuo* (Summary of the Pure Land) by Weng Shuyuan.
The Great Master Lianchi extensively gathered accounts of those who, since the Jin and Tang dynasties, attained rebirth in the Pure Land through the practice of *nien-fo*.
He composed biographies and eulogies for each, following the style of historical records, totaling one hundred and sixty-six individuals.

These were compiled into a single volume titled the *Wangsheng ji* (Collection on Rebirth), which has long been in circulation. Among these, there are four individuals whom Shu-yuan personally encountered; all were natives of Changshu. The first was...

A monk from the Geuntong Temple at the North Gate daily carried a wooden board through the streets and alleys, loudly chanting that impermanence is swift and urging everyone to mindfully recite the Buddha’s name;
the public did not find this particularly strange. In the third month of spring in the thirteenth year of the Ming Chongzhen era (the Gengchen year), he took leave of all his neighbors.
My uncle Yuan was eight years old at the time, playing at the temple gate when the monk stroked his head and said:
"Little Master, you have recited the Buddha’s name well. This old monk departs now. At first, Shuye did not understand why;

however, the next day, the monk offered incense before the Buddha, joined his palms in recitation, and passed away while sitting upright. Another was an elderly woman from south of the city whose surname was Chen.
She was over seventy years of age and made her living by spinning cotton yarn. As she worked, she would recite the Buddha’s name to the sound of her spinning wheel, doing so all day long.
She remained silent. In this manner, thirty years passed. One day, she suddenly said to her son, "Son, do you not see the banners, streamers, and jeweled canopies in the sky?
She then clapped her hands and laughed loudly. Having taken water herself to bathe, she joined her palms and passed away amidst a crowd of onlookers as dense as a wall.
When Shu Yuan went to look, he saw only the old woman sitting upright and motionless within the room.
A fragrance, pure and penetrating, permeated the air; it was not of this world. It was the summer of the fourth month in the tenth year of the Shunzhi era (the Gui-si year).
One was Chan Master Chongwen, a grand-disciple of the Elder of Yunqi. He resided in a quiet chamber in Nan-zhu Village and was fifty years of age.
Having lost the sight of both eyes, he devoted himself single-mindedly to the recitation of the Buddha’s name. Every night, he ascended the seat to perform *yujia* (meditative yoga).

He consumed *gā* for three years without ceasing. On the fourteenth day of the third month in the fifteenth year of Shunzhi (the Wuxu year), his disciple Xingxian came to me and said, "The Master will depart for the West tomorrow;
he has specifically sent me to bid you farewell. I hurried there at once.
It was already dark night, and as the city gates were closed, he could not go out. At dawn the following day, he went to his teacher’s residence;
more than thirty people, both monastics and laypeople, had gathered there. The teacher sat upon a couch and commanded his disciples to recite one scroll of the *Amitābha Sūtra*.
Having finished his recitation, he entered into stillness. Within the room, the fragrance of chrysanthemums was perceived for three days without dispersing.

One was Master Zhinan; the Master had been engaged in study for many years. He resided at the Wuwang Hermitage within Dongta Temple, sitting in silence throughout the day while reciting the Buddha’s name.
If people gave him money, he would immediately redistribute it to others. His nature was straightforward and open; he felt no slight attachment to anything. There was a *zhī* fungus...

Several virtuous laymen from Tangli had long since taken refuge in the Master. In the sixth month of the summer in the thirtieth year of the Kangxi era (the Xinwei year), they entered the city to visit him.
The Master said to them, "On the fifth day of next month, I shall part from all my donors. The group went as scheduled;
the Master spoke no other words, but only exhorted them to recite the Buddha’s name. He then sat in the lotus posture and passed away. I am his son, Youzhi Long.

While staying in a study hut, I personally witnessed these matters. Since the passing of Master Yunqi, the lineage of the Pure Land dharma-gate has been sparse throughout the Jiang and Zhejiang regions.
In Changshu, there is Puren Temple, which was restored by Mr. Lu Xuzhong, the Minister of Personnel;
and in Jintan, there is Jingtu Temple, where the brothers of Mr. Li Xiaoyan, the Minister of Revenue, donated their own residence to establish as a monastery.
Among those who took up residence at both monasteries were the four great masters Jie-liu, Shen-ye, Xia-biao, and He-qu.
All possessed great vows and promoted the Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation to guide future generations; they were diligent and courageous, and students flocked to follow them as their models.
After Master Jie-liu turned his head toward the West, there was the elder son of Mr. Fusang, the Grand Marshal Sun.
Han Chen was summoned by the authorities of the underworld. After being dead for one day and night, he awoke and said:
"While I was detained before the Lord King Yama, I suddenly beheld a light illuminating the heavens amidst the darkness.

Fragrant flowers were spread across the void as King Yama prostrated himself on the ground to welcome the Great Master Xigui—this was none other than Master Juegong. Because I was touched by the Master’s radiance, I was subsequently released."

Upon his return, on the same day, the son of the Wu family outside the South Gate died and was revived after the night had passed. He recounted what he had seen, exactly as the monk’s disciple had described.

The Master himself bore calluses from long travel and underwent great hardship and austerity; he raised funds to cast an iron image of Maitreya sixteen feet tall, which was only completed after three years.
A local sorcerer in Changshu, suspecting the Master possessed surplus wealth, lusted for it and instigated a legal case against him. The Master simply drew his staff and departed.

He set out on his journey. At that time, Master Xia was residing at Jingtusi (Pure Land Temple). Upon hearing that Master Shen was traveling there, he said with joy, "I have finally found the right person for my abbot's quarters.

On the sixth day of the tenth month of the year Yihai, he welcomed Master Shen into the temple. Two days later, Master Xia recited a verse to bid farewell to the assembly, sat upon a pile of firewood, and immolated himself by lighting the flames.
The great multitude watched in awe and lamented, weeping with grief at such an unprecedented occurrence. Master Shen...
Once Master Gong had settled at Jingtu, he invited Master He to reside at Puren. The Dharma banners of these two sites stood facing one another, drawing the reverent devotion of those near and far.
Among the people within the realm, many were moved by their reputation and arose to follow them;
they succeeded to the Dharma seat of Yunqi and boarded the compassionate vessel of the great ocean, with those seeking the Way arriving in succession between Jintan and Changshu. This was Master He.
May you, sir, continue to exert yourself!

This letter to the layman Mr. Mao Jingyuan was written by Dharma Master Siqi in the third lunar month, shortly after he had returned from Siming and visited the layman; unfortunately, he encountered you when you were away, leaving him with a sense of regret.

I departed and returned to Long [Mountain] some month ago. Because several friends urged me to lecture on the *Lotus Sūtra*, I specifically came to Hangzhou to request the scripture, which has allowed me to send this letter to you.
The completion of the bridge by your honor may be called a most magnificent achievement;
yet, your heart, O Layman, delights in goodness without weariness—once one good deed is finished, you immediately undertake another.
"Excellent! It is indeed excellent. Yet, what does it avail regarding the great matter of birth and death?

If one does not regard the great matter of birth and death as urgent, but instead applies oneself diligently to doing good—so that the virtuous deeds performed are as vast as Mount Sumeru—they are all merely karmic conditions for birth and death;
when will there ever be an end to them? The more virtuous deeds one performs, the broader becomes the cycle of birth and death. A single thought of attachment binds one for ten thousand kalpas."
Are you not afraid? Layman, you have long since penetrated the public cases of this world, and you have long since cultivated the pure karma of the Western Paradise.
Yet, your resolve regarding birth and death is not urgent; you cannot cast off domestic attachments; you cannot decline social obligations;

and your mind for reciting the Buddha’s name is not single-minded. Why is this? Is it because the root of fame has not been severed? Or is it because the bonds of affection still entangle you? Regarding these two...

Those who wish to do so should exercise careful scrutiny. If one does not decisively sever all domestic and worldly concerns with a single stroke and exert one’s full strength in upholding the six-character Great Name, it will be difficult to hope for liberation from this Sahā world and rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang).

It would be even more difficult to seek liberation from birth and death without being reborn in An-yang, or to seek to avoid falling into the lower realms without being liberated from birth and death. Even if one...
To have been born twice and yet not lose one’s human form—what does this accomplish? Alas! Layman, your wisdom is so clear and sharp;
your family fortune is so abundant; your descendants are so virtuous and capable;
everything suits your heart’s desire—and yet you still cannot let go of myriad concerns to single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name. Is Heaven betraying you, or are you betraying Heaven? No.
To make mindfulness of the Buddha one’s primary concern while making worldly minor virtues one’s priority;

to fail to regard the great matter of birth and death as foremost while regarding the blessings and rewards of humans and devas as foremost—this is to be ignorant of what comes first and what comes last.

For you, Layman, the urgent task today is simply to decline all social affairs and focus the mind single-mindedly on mindfulness of the Buddha. Furthermore, to add the two characters for "fasting and precepts" (zhāijì) will make it even more complete.
Excellence! Generally speaking, the Western Buddha-land cannot be reached by means of ordinary, scattered good deeds;
the cycle of birth and death through ten thousand kalpas cannot be escaped through complacency or indolence. Impermanence is swift; it arrives as suddenly as morning turns to evening.
How can one not prepare for it early? Among those I know personally, they are very few; yet among those I do know, I seek someone with whom I may discuss this matter.
Those who do so are exceedingly few. Setting aside the one layman, who is there that looks toward this with deep expectation?
If you do not discard the words because of the person, I hope you will exert yourself. If you say, "I am unable," then there is nothing that can be done.

To instruct a practitioner of Chan, the single phrase "Namu Amida Butsu" is itself the public case (kōan). There is no other deliberation; it is resolved directly and immediately, like a great mass of fire.
To touch it is to be burned, like the sword Ta’a; to strike it is to be consumed. The eighty-four thousand treasuries of the Dharma are fully contained within six characters;
the thousand-seven hundred entangled vines are severed with a single stroke. Whether Buddhas or others find it unpleasant to hear, I myself recollect it heart and mind.
Please do not speak at length; simply maintain single-mindedness without distraction.
